weeks.title: Week 1: Consolidation Accounting & Multi-Entity Reporting
weeks.lessonHtml:
Week 1: Consolidation Accounting & Multi-Entity Reporting

Learning Objectives

By the end of this week, you will be able to:

  • Understand when consolidation accounting is required under ASC 810
  • Prepare consolidating elimination entries for parent-subsidiary relationships
  • Account for non-controlling interests in partially-owned subsidiaries
  • Apply the equity method for joint ventures and investments
  • Prepare consolidated financial statements for construction holding companies
  • Navigate variable interest entity (VIE) rules for special purpose entities
  • Understand intercompany transactions and proper elimination procedures

Introduction: Why Construction Companies Use Multiple Entities

Construction companies frequently operate through multiple legal entities for various strategic reasons:

  • Risk Isolation: Separate entities for high-risk projects or business lines
  • Licensing Requirements: Different licenses for different trades or states
  • Tax Optimization: Structuring for state tax advantages or federal tax benefits
  • Joint Ventures: Partnering with other contractors on large projects
  • Ownership Structure: Family ownership across multiple generations
  • Acquisition Strategy: Keeping acquired companies as separate subsidiaries
  • Bonding Capacity: Separate entities to maximize surety credit

Common Multi-Entity Structures in Construction

Example: Summit Construction Group

  • Summit Holdings, Inc. (Parent Company)
    • Summit General Contracting, LLC (100% owned) - Commercial construction
    • Summit Residential Builders, LLC (100% owned) - Residential construction
    • Mountain Mechanical, Inc. (80% owned) - HVAC and plumbing
    • Alpine Equipment Leasing, LLC (100% owned) - Equipment rental to affiliates
    • Summit-Jones JV, LLC (50% owned) - Joint venture for highway project

Consolidation Requirements:

  • Summit General, Summit Residential, Alpine Equipment: Full consolidation (100% ownership)
  • Mountain Mechanical: Consolidate with non-controlling interest (80% ownership)
  • Summit-Jones JV: Equity method accounting (50% ownership, no control)

Section 1: Consolidation Requirements Under ASC 810

1.1 The Control Principle

ASC 810 (Consolidation) requires consolidation when one entity has a controlling financial interest in another entity.

Control Generally Means:

  • Ownership of >50% of voting shares (voting interest model), OR
  • Power to direct activities that most significantly impact economic performance + obligation to absorb losses or right to receive benefits (variable interest entity model)

1.2 Voting Interest Model

Under the traditional voting interest model:

Ownership %Accounting TreatmentFinancial Reporting
0-20% Cost method or Fair Value Investment account on balance sheet; dividends as income
20-50% Equity method Investment account adjusted for share of earnings/losses
>50% Full consolidation Combine all assets, liabilities, revenues, expenses

1.3 Variable Interest Entity (VIE) Model

A Variable Interest Entity is an entity that either:

  1. Lacks sufficient equity to finance activities without additional subordinated financial support, OR
  2. Has equity holders that lack decision-making ability, obligation to absorb losses, or right to receive returns

Common VIEs in Construction:

  • Special purpose entities for specific projects
  • Joint ventures with unequal profit/loss sharing
  • Entities where voting rights don't align with economics
  • Project companies with non-recourse debt

The primary beneficiary (entity with power + economic interest) must consolidate the VIE.

Example 1: VIE Analysis for Project SPE

Scenario: Regional Developer LLC creates Project Sunrise SPE to develop a $50M mixed-use building.

SPE Structure:

  • Total project cost: $50 million
  • Equity contributed: $5 million (10%)
    • Regional Developer: $2.5M (50%)
    • Passive Investors: $2.5M (50%)
  • Non-recourse project debt: $45 million
  • Regional Developer also serves as general contractor

VIE Analysis:

Is it a VIE?

  1. Equity at risk: $5M ÷ $50M = 10% (likely insufficient to finance activities without subordinated support)
  2. Passive investors lack decision-making ability (Regional Developer makes all decisions)
  3. Conclusion: YES, this is a VIE

Who is Primary Beneficiary?

  • Power: Regional Developer has power to direct activities (manages project, makes all decisions)
  • Economics: Regional Developer has 50% equity plus fees as general contractor
  • Conclusion: Regional Developer is primary beneficiary and must consolidate Project Sunrise SPE

Financial Statement Impact:

  • Consolidate $50M in assets (land, construction in progress)
  • Consolidate $45M in project debt
  • Show $2.5M non-controlling interest in equity
  • Recognize construction revenue and costs as GC

Section 2: Basic Consolidation Process

2.1 Consolidation Steps

The consolidation process involves six key steps:

  1. Individual Financials: Gather standalone financial statements for parent and subsidiaries
  2. Alignment: Ensure consistent accounting policies and reporting periods
  3. Translation: Translate foreign subsidiary financials if applicable
  4. Combination: Add together all assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses line-by-line
  5. Eliminations: Remove intercompany transactions and balances
  6. Non-Controlling Interest: Calculate and present NCI for partially-owned subsidiaries

2.2 Investment Elimination Entry

The fundamental consolidation entry eliminates the parent's investment account against the subsidiary's equity accounts.

Example 2: Basic Investment Elimination - 100% Ownership

Scenario: Summit Holdings acquired 100% of Alpine Equipment for $2,500,000 on January 1, 2024.

Alpine Equipment's Equity at Acquisition:

  • Common Stock: $500,000
  • Retained Earnings: $1,500,000
  • Total Equity: $2,000,000

Purchase Price Analysis:

  • Purchase price: $2,500,000
  • Book value acquired: $2,000,000
  • Excess over book value (Goodwill): $500,000

Consolidation Elimination Entry (at acquisition):

Dr. Common Stock - Alpine                         $500,000
Dr. Retained Earnings - Alpine                  $1,500,000
Dr. Goodwill                                      $500,000
    Cr. Investment in Alpine Equipment                    $2,500,000
(To eliminate investment account against subsidiary equity)

Result: The investment account disappears from the consolidated balance sheet, replaced by Alpine's individual assets and liabilities plus goodwill.

2.3 Intercompany Transaction Eliminations

All transactions between consolidated entities must be eliminated to avoid double-counting.

Common Intercompany Transactions in Construction:

Transaction TypeWhy It OccursElimination Required
Equipment rental Equipment subsidiary rents to construction entity Eliminate rental revenue/expense
Management fees Parent charges subsidiaries for services Eliminate fee revenue/expense
Interest on intercompany loans Parent lends to subsidiary for projects Eliminate interest income/expense and loan balances
Subcontract work One entity subcontracts to sister company Eliminate subcontract revenue/cost
Asset transfers Transfer equipment between entities Eliminate gain/loss on transfer

Example 3: Equipment Rental Elimination

Scenario: Alpine Equipment Leasing (subsidiary) rented equipment to Summit General Contracting (sister company) for $240,000 during 2024.

Individual Company Records:

Alpine Equipment (Rental Company):

Dr. Cash                                          $240,000
    Cr. Equipment Rental Revenue                          $240,000

Summit General (Renter):

Dr. Equipment Rental Expense - Project 401       $240,000
    Cr. Cash                                              $240,000

Consolidation Elimination Entry:

Dr. Equipment Rental Revenue                     $240,000
    Cr. Equipment Rental Expense                          $240,000
(To eliminate intercompany rental transactions)

Consolidated Result: From the group's perspective, the company simply moved equipment between projects. No external revenue or expense occurred.

Section 3: Non-Controlling Interest (Minority Interest)

3.1 Accounting for NCI

When a parent owns less than 100% of a subsidiary, the portion owned by others is called Non-Controlling Interest (formerly "minority interest").

NCI Presentation:

  • Balance Sheet: NCI shown as separate component of equity
  • Income Statement: NCI's share of subsidiary earnings shown as deduction
  • Full Consolidation: 100% of subsidiary assets/liabilities consolidated regardless of ownership %

Example 4: Non-Controlling Interest Calculation

Scenario: Summit Holdings owns 80% of Mountain Mechanical, acquired for $4,000,000 when book value was $4,500,000 (fair value = book value).

Mountain Mechanical 2024 Results:

  • Net Income: $850,000
  • Dividends Paid: $300,000
  • Ending Retained Earnings: $3,200,000

NCI Calculations:

NCI Share of Net Income:

  • Net income: $850,000 × 20% = $170,000

NCI Share of Dividends:

  • Dividends: $300,000 × 20% = $60,000

NCI Balance Sheet Amount:

  • Beginning NCI (20% × $4,500,000): $900,000
  • Plus: NCI share of income: $170,000
  • Less: NCI share of dividends: ($60,000)
  • Ending NCI: $1,010,000

Consolidated Income Statement (partial):

Revenues                                      $12,450,000
Cost of Revenues                              (8,920,000)
Operating Expenses                            (2,130,000)
                                              ___________
Net Income                                     1,400,000
  Less: Net Income Attributable to NCI          (170,000)
                                              ___________
Net Income Attributable to Summit Holdings   $1,230,000
                                              ===========

Consolidated Balance Sheet (equity section):

Common Stock                                   $5,000,000
Retained Earnings                              18,750,000
  Total Summit Holdings Equity                 23,750,000
Non-Controlling Interest                        1,010,000
                                              ___________
Total Equity                                  $24,760,000
                                              ===========

Section 4: Equity Method Accounting

4.1 When Equity Method Applies

The equity method is used when an investor has significant influence but not control over an investee:

  • Ownership: Typically 20-50% of voting stock
  • Significant Influence: Ability to influence operating and financial policies
  • Common in Construction: Joint ventures, partnerships, minority investments

4.2 Equity Method Procedures

Initial Recognition:

Dr. Investment in Affiliate                [Cost]
    Cr. Cash                                          [Cost]

Periodic Adjustments:

  • Share of Earnings: Increase investment account
  • Share of Losses: Decrease investment account
  • Dividends Received: Decrease investment account (return of capital)

Example 5: Equity Method for Joint Venture

Scenario: Summit Holdings forms Summit-Jones JV with Jones Construction, each contributing $5M for 50% ownership. The JV was formed to build a $180M highway project.

Year 1 (2024) Activity:

January 1, 2024 - Initial Investment:

Dr. Investment in Summit-Jones JV              $5,000,000
    Cr. Cash                                            $5,000,000
(Summit's 50% equity contribution)

JV Operations for 2024:

  • Contract revenue: $45,000,000
  • Costs incurred: $38,000,000
  • Operating expenses: $3,200,000
  • Net income: $3,800,000
  • Cash distributions to partners: $2,000,000 ($1,000,000 each)

Summit's Equity Method Entries:

Record share of JV income:

Dr. Investment in Summit-Jones JV              $1,900,000
    Cr. Equity in Earnings of JV                        $1,900,000
(50% × $3,800,000 net income)

Record cash distribution:

Dr. Cash                                       $1,000,000
    Cr. Investment in Summit-Jones JV                   $1,000,000
(Cash distribution reduces investment account)

Investment Account Balance 12/31/2024:

  • Beginning balance: $5,000,000
  • Plus: Share of income: $1,900,000
  • Less: Distribution: ($1,000,000)
  • Ending balance: $5,900,000

Income Statement Presentation:

Operating Income                               $8,200,000
Other Income:
  Equity in Earnings of JV                      1,900,000
                                              ___________
Income Before Tax                             $10,100,000

Balance Sheet Presentation:

Assets:
  Current Assets                              $42,500,000
  Property and Equipment                       28,750,000
  Investment in Summit-Jones JV (equity method) 5,900,000
  Other Assets                                  3,850,000
                                              ___________
Total Assets                                  $81,000,000

4.3 Equity Method vs. Proportionate Consolidation

Some jurisdictions allow proportionate consolidation for joint ventures, but U.S. GAAP requires equity method.

MethodBalance SheetIncome StatementU.S. GAAP?
Equity Method Single line: Investment in JV Single line: Equity in earnings Required for JVs
Proportionate Consolidation Include share of each asset/liability Include share of each revenue/expense Not permitted

Section 5: Intercompany Profit Elimination

5.1 Downstream Transactions

When parent sells to subsidiary (downstream), any unrealized profit must be eliminated from consolidated statements.

Example 6: Downstream Sale - Equipment Transfer

Scenario: Summit Holdings sells a used excavator to Summit General Contracting (100% owned subsidiary).

  • Summit Holdings' book value: $125,000
  • Sale price to Summit General: $160,000
  • Gain recorded by Summit Holdings: $35,000

Why Eliminate? From a consolidated perspective, the company still owns the excavator. The $35,000 gain represents intercompany profit that hasn't been realized through a sale to an external party.

Consolidation Elimination Entry:

Dr. Gain on Sale of Equipment                    $35,000
    Cr. Equipment                                         $35,000
(To eliminate unrealized gain on intercompany sale)

Impact: Consolidated equipment balance shows $125,000 (original cost), not $160,000 (transfer price).

When is it realized? When Summit General either:

  1. Depreciates the equipment (gain realized proportionately), or
  2. Sells equipment to external party (gain realized immediately)

5.2 Upstream Transactions

When subsidiary sells to parent (upstream) and there's NCI, elimination is allocated between controlling and non-controlling interest.

Example 7: Upstream Sale with NCI

Scenario: Mountain Mechanical (80% owned) performs $500,000 in HVAC subcontract work for Summit General at 25% markup.

  • Mountain Mechanical's cost: $400,000
  • Billed to Summit General: $500,000
  • Gross profit: $100,000
  • Work remains in Summit General's WIP (not yet billed to customer)

Unrealized Profit Analysis:

  • Total unrealized profit: $100,000
  • Allocate to controlling interest (80%): $80,000
  • Allocate to NCI (20%): $20,000

Consolidation Elimination Entry:

Dr. Subcontract Revenue (Mountain Mechanical)   $500,000
    Cr. Subcontract Expense (Summit General)            $500,000
(Eliminate intercompany transaction)

Dr. Cost of Revenue (Mountain Mechanical)       $100,000
    Cr. Work in Progress (Summit General)               $100,000
(Eliminate unrealized profit in WIP)

NCI Adjustment:

Dr. Non-Controlling Interest                     $20,000
Dr. Retained Earnings                             $80,000
    Cr. Cost of Revenue                                  $100,000
(Allocate elimination between NCI and controlling interest)

Section 6: Consolidation Worksheet

6.1 Worksheet Format

Most consolidations are prepared using a worksheet with these columns:

  1. Parent company trial balance
  2. Subsidiary trial balance(s)
  3. Eliminations - Debit
  4. Eliminations - Credit
  5. Consolidated balances

Example 8: Simple Consolidation Worksheet

  • Eliminate Investment in Alpine ($2,500,000) against Alpine's equity ($2,000,000)
  • Recognize goodwill for excess purchase price ($500,000)

Practice Problems - Week 1

Problem 1: Basic Consolidation Entry

Regional Builders acquired 100% of Specialty Contractors on January 1, 2025 for $8,500,000 cash.

Specialty Contractors' Balance Sheet at Acquisition:

  • Total Assets: $12,000,000
  • Total Liabilities: $5,000,000
  • Common Stock: $2,000,000
  • Retained Earnings: $5,000,000

Required:

  1. Calculate the book value acquired
  2. Calculate goodwill or bargain purchase gain
  3. Prepare the consolidation elimination entry at acquisition
  4. What would consolidated total assets be if Regional Builders had $45M in assets before acquisition?

Problem 2: Non-Controlling Interest

Summit Holdings acquired 75% of Mountain Mechanical on January 1, 2024 for $6,000,000 when book value was $7,200,000 (fair value = book value).

Mountain Mechanical 2024-2025 Activity:

YearNet IncomeDividends Paid
2024$1,200,000$400,000
2025$1,450,000$500,000

Required:

  1. Calculate beginning NCI (1/1/2024)
  2. Calculate NCI share of 2024 income and dividends
  3. Calculate ending NCI (12/31/2024)
  4. Calculate ending NCI (12/31/2025)
  5. Prepare the equity section of consolidated balance sheet at 12/31/2025

Problem 3: Equity Method Accounting

Apex Construction owns 40% of Midwest Joint Venture. On January 1, 2025, Apex contributed $10,000,000 for its 40% interest.

MJV 2025 Operations:

  • Revenue: $75,000,000
  • Expenses: $68,500,000
  • Net Income: $6,500,000
  • Cash distributions to partners: $4,000,000 total

Required:

  1. Prepare Apex's journal entry for initial investment
  2. Calculate Apex's share of MJV income
  3. Calculate Apex's share of cash distribution
  4. Prepare entries to record share of income and distribution
  5. Calculate Investment in MJV balance at 12/31/2025
  6. Show how this appears on Apex's income statement and balance sheet

Problem 4: Intercompany Elimination

Construction Holding Co. owns 100% of Equipment Rental subsidiary. During 2025:

  • Equipment Rental charged Construction Co. $1,200,000 for equipment rentals
  • Equipment Rental's cost/depreciation on rented equipment: $750,000
  • Construction Holding charged Equipment Rental $180,000 management fees
  • Construction Holding had $95,000 actual cost providing management services

Required:

  1. Prepare elimination entry for equipment rentals
  2. Prepare elimination entry for management fees
  3. Calculate consolidated operating income impact
  4. Explain why eliminations are necessary

Key Takeaways - Week 1

Essential Concepts to Remember

  • Control Principle: Consolidate when owning >50% voting shares OR when primary beneficiary of VIE
  • Full Consolidation: Include 100% of subsidiary assets/liabilities regardless of ownership percentage
  • NCI Presentation: Show separately in equity section; deduct NCI's share of income on income statement
  • Equity Method: Use for 20-50% ownership; adjust investment for share of earnings/losses and dividends
  • Intercompany Eliminations: Remove ALL transactions between consolidated entities to avoid double-counting
  • Goodwill: Excess of purchase price over book value acquired; test for impairment annually
  • VIE Rules: Project SPEs and certain JVs may require consolidation even without majority voting control
  • Upstream vs. Downstream: Upstream sales from subsidiary to parent require NCI allocation of profit elimination

flashcards.question: What is the primary indicator for consolidation under ASC 810?
flashcards.answer: Controlling financial interest - either >50% voting stock (voting interest entity model) or being the primary beneficiary of a Variable Interest Entity (VIE model). Control means the power to direct the entity's activities that most significantly impact economic performance.

flashcards.question: What is a Variable Interest Entity (VIE)?
flashcards.answer: An entity that lacks sufficient equity to finance its activities without additional subordinated financial support, or where equity holders lack decision-making ability, obligation to absorb losses, or right to receive returns. Common in construction: project SPEs, joint ventures with minimal equity, entities with non-substantive voting rights.

flashcards.question: What are the two requirements to be the primary beneficiary of a VIE?
flashcards.answer: (1) Power to direct the activities that most significantly impact the VIE's economic performance, AND (2) Obligation to absorb losses or right to receive benefits that could potentially be significant to the VIE. BOTH must be present to consolidate.

flashcards.question: What is the investment elimination entry on acquisition date?
flashcards.answer: DR: Subsidiary's Equity accounts (Common Stock, APIC, Retained Earnings) at book value, DR: Goodwill (if purchase price > book value); CR: Investment in Subsidiary account at cost. This eliminates the parent's investment account and the subsidiary's equity to avoid double-counting.

flashcards.question: What is Non-Controlling Interest (NCI) and how is it measured?
flashcards.answer: NCI represents the equity in a subsidiary not attributable to the parent. ASC 810 allows measurement at: (1) Fair value (full goodwill method), or (2) Proportionate share of identifiable net assets. NCI is presented in the equity section of consolidated balance sheet, separate from parent equity.

flashcards.question: How are intercompany sales eliminated in consolidation?
flashcards.answer: Eliminate both the sale and the cost: DR: Sales; CR: Cost of Goods Sold (for the full intercompany transaction amount). If inventory remains unsold at year-end, also eliminate unrealized profit: DR: COGS; CR: Inventory (for profit in ending inventory). 100% of intercompany profit is eliminated regardless of NCI %.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between downstream and upstream intercompany transactions?
flashcards.answer: Downstream = Parent sells to Subsidiary (profit in parent's books, elimination reduces parent income). Upstream = Subsidiary sells to Parent (profit in subsidiary's books, elimination allocated between parent and NCI proportionately). Direction affects which party's income is reduced by the elimination.

flashcards.question: How does the equity method work for investments with significant influence (20-50%)?
flashcards.answer: Investment account increases by investor's share of investee income and decreases by dividends received: Investment beginning balance + (Ownership % × Investee Net Income) - (Ownership % × Dividends) = Investment ending balance. Creates 'one-line consolidation' - investor reports its share without combining line items.

flashcards.question: How are intercompany dividends eliminated in consolidation?
flashcards.answer: DR: Dividends Declared (subsidiary's books); CR: Investment in Subsidiary or Dividend Income (parent's portion) and NCI (their portion). Total elimination equals 100% of subsidiary's dividend. Prevents double-counting since subsidiary's retained earnings are already included in consolidated statements.

flashcards.question: What is excess depreciation/amortization in consolidation?
flashcards.answer: When purchase price exceeds book value, fair value adjustments on subsidiary's assets must be depreciated/amortized. Example: Building FV $3M, BV $2M, 10-year life → Annual excess depreciation = $1M ÷ 10 = $100K. Reduces consolidated net income and is allocated between parent and NCI based on ownership percentages.

quiz.question: Under ASC 810, which of the following is the PRIMARY indicator that consolidation is required?
options: Ownership of more than 25% of voting stock
Significant influence over operating decisions
Controlling financial interest (>50% voting stock or primary beneficiary of VIE)
Ability to appoint one board member
quiz.explanation: ASC 810 requires consolidation when an entity has a controlling financial interest, which typically means owning more than 50% of voting stock (voting interest entity model) or being the primary beneficiary of a Variable Interest Entity (VIE model). Significant influence (20-50% ownership) uses equity method accounting, not consolidation.

quiz.question: Mountain Construction owns 80% of Valley Contractors, acquired for $2M when Valley's equity was $2M. Valley reports net income of $500K and pays dividends of $100K. What is Mountain's equity in Valley's earnings?
quiz.explanation: Under consolidation, the parent recognizes 100% of the subsidiary's revenues and expenses. The non-controlling interest (NCI) gets their 20% share ($500K × 20% = $100K) on the consolidated income statement, but Mountain's equity in earnings is the full $500K net income minus the $100K NCI share = $400K. This is different from the equity method where only the proportionate share (80%) would be recorded.

quiz.question: A construction company creates a Special Purpose Entity (SPE) to hold a $10M project. The SPE is 90% debt-financed by a bank, with the construction company providing a 10% equity investment and guaranteeing the debt. Under the VIE model, who is likely the primary beneficiary?
options: The bank, because they provided 90% of financing
The construction company, because they have power and absorb risks/benefits
Neither - the SPE consolidates separately
Both equally share consolidation responsibility
quiz.explanation: Under ASC 810-10-25, the primary beneficiary is the entity with: (1) power to direct activities that most significantly impact economic performance, and (2) obligation to absorb losses or right to receive benefits that could be significant. The construction company likely has operational control and the debt guarantee means they absorb losses, making them the primary beneficiary required to consolidate the SPE, despite only 10% equity ownership.

quiz.question: On the date of acquisition, what is the correct elimination entry for a parent's $3M investment in a subsidiary with $2.5M book value equity (assuming 100% acquisition)?
options: DR: Investment $3M; CR: Equity $3M
DR: Equity $2.5M, Goodwill $500K; CR: Investment $3M
DR: Cash $3M; CR: Investment $3M
DR: Equity $3M; CR: Investment $2.5M, Gain $500K
quiz.explanation: The investment elimination entry removes the parent's Investment account and the subsidiary's equity accounts, with the difference recorded as Goodwill (if purchase price exceeds book value) or Bargain Purchase Gain (if book value exceeds price). Here: DR: Common Stock, APIC, Retained Earnings (totaling $2.5M), DR: Goodwill $500K; CR: Investment in Subsidiary $3M.

quiz.question: Non-controlling interest (NCI) should be measured at acquisition date using which approach under ASC 810?
options: Always at fair value (full goodwill method)
Always at proportionate share of identifiable net assets
Either fair value or proportionate share, as an accounting policy choice
Book value of subsidiary equity × NCI percentage
quiz.explanation: ASC 810-10-30-2 allows acquirers to choose between: (1) Fair value method - NCI measured at fair value (recognizes full goodwill attributable to both controlling and non-controlling interests), or (2) Proportionate share method - NCI measured at proportionate share of identifiable net assets (recognizes only parent's share of goodwill). This is an accounting policy choice made acquisition by acquisition.

quiz.question: A parent sells inventory to its 70%-owned subsidiary at cost plus 30% markup. At year-end, 40% remains in subsidiary's inventory. The parent's cost was $100K. What is the correct intercompany profit elimination?
options: DR: Sales $130K; CR: COGS $130K
DR: COGS $12K; CR: Inventory $12K
DR: Sales $156K; CR: COGS $100K, Inventory $56K
DR: Retained Earnings $12K; CR: Inventory $12K
quiz.explanation: Unrealized intercompany profit in ending inventory must be eliminated. Calculation: Parent's cost $100K × 30% markup = $30K intercompany profit × 40% remaining in inventory = $12K to eliminate. Entry: DR: COGS (or Equity in Subsidiary Earnings) $12K; CR: Inventory $12K. The full $12K is eliminated because consolidation eliminates ALL intercompany profit, regardless of NCI percentage. In downstream sales (parent to subsidiary), the adjustment reduces parent's income.

quiz.question: Peak Construction owns 35% of Valley JV and uses the equity method. Valley reports $1M net income and $200K dividends. Peak's investment had an initial cost of $3M when Valley's equity was $8M. What is Peak's year-end investment balance if the beginning balance was $3M?
quiz.explanation: Under equity method: Investment increases by proportionate share of income and decreases by dividends received. Calculation: Beginning $3M + (35% × $1M income) - (35% × $200K dividends) = $3M + $350K - $70K = $3,280K. The investment account is adjusted for the investor's share of earnings (increasing) and dividends (decreasing), creating a 'one-line consolidation' effect.

quiz.question: When a subsidiary pays a $300K dividend to its parent (80% ownership) and outside shareholders (20% NCI), what is the consolidation elimination entry?
options: DR: Dividend Income $300K; CR: Cash $300K
DR: Dividend Income $240K; CR: Dividends Declared $240K
DR: Dividends Declared $300K; CR: Cash $240K, NCI $60K
No elimination entry needed - dividends reduce retained earnings
quiz.explanation: In consolidation, intercompany dividends must be eliminated because they represent transfers within the consolidated entity. The subsidiary's Dividends Declared account ($300K) is eliminated against: (1) the parent's dividend received (shown as reduction in Investment or Dividend Income) of $240K (80%), and (2) the NCI's share of $60K (20%). Entry: DR: Dividends Declared $300K; CR: Investment in Subsidiary (or Dividend Income) $240K, NCI $60K.

quiz.question: Cascade Construction holds a 40% interest in Summit JV (equity method). Summit sells equipment to Cascade for $150K; Summit's cost was $100K. Cascade is depreciating the equipment over 5 years (straight-line). What adjustment is needed in Year 1?
options: Reduce equity income by $50K (full profit)
Reduce equity income by $20K (40% of $50K profit)
Reduce equity income by $16K ($20K profit less $4K realized through depreciation)
No adjustment - arm's length transaction
quiz.explanation: Upstream intercompany profit (subsidiary to investor) must be deferred and amortized. Step 1: Intercompany profit = $50K × 40% investor share = $20K to defer. Step 2: Realized through use = $50K excess ÷ 5 years = $10K per year × 40% = $4K. Step 3: Net deferral in Year 1 = $20K - $4K = $16K. Entry: DR: Equity in Investee Income $16K; CR: Investment in Investee $16K. Each year, $4K will be 'realized' and recognized.

quiz.question: A wholly-owned subsidiary issues $2M in bonds at par to the parent company. How is this reflected in consolidated financial statements?
options: Liability on consolidated balance sheet of $2M
Asset (bond investment) and liability (bonds payable) both shown at $2M
Completely eliminated - no balance sheet impact
Shown as intercompany loan with footnote disclosure
quiz.explanation: Intercompany debt must be completely eliminated in consolidation. The parent's Bond Investment and the subsidiary's Bonds Payable accounts offset each other. Consolidation entry: DR: Bonds Payable $2M; CR: Investment in Bonds $2M. From an external perspective, the consolidated entity cannot owe money to itself. Any intercompany interest income/expense is also eliminated from the consolidated income statement.

quiz.question: Under ASC 810, how should NCI be presented on the consolidated balance sheet?
options: As a liability between liabilities and equity
In the equity section, separately from parent's equity
As a reduction from the Investment account
In a mezzanine section between liabilities and equity
quiz.explanation: ASC 810-10-45-16 requires NCI to be presented in the equity section of the consolidated balance sheet, separately from the parent's equity. Previously (pre-2009), NCI was shown in a 'mezzanine' section between liabilities and equity. The current standard recognizes NCI as ownership interest, though separate disclosure is required to distinguish parent shareholders' equity from NCI.

quiz.question: Mountain Construction acquires 100% of Valley Contractors for $5M. Valley's book value is $4M, but a building with book value of $2M has fair value of $3M. Assuming 10-year remaining life, what is the annual excess depreciation in consolidation?
options: $0 - no adjustment needed
quiz.explanation: Fair value adjustments must be depreciated/amortized in consolidation. Step 1: Purchase price $5M - Book value $4M = $1M excess. Step 2: Fair value adjustment on building = $1M ($3M FV - $2M BV). Step 3: Excess depreciation = $1M ÷ 10 years = $100K per year. This additional depreciation reduces consolidated net income and is allocated between parent and NCI (though NCI is 0% here, so all affects parent).

quiz.question: Which financial statement shows the change in NCI during the year?
options: Consolidated balance sheet only
Consolidated statement of changes in equity
Consolidated income statement only
Notes to financial statements only
quiz.explanation: ASC 810-10-45-20 requires a consolidated statement of changes in equity showing: (1) beginning NCI balance, (2) NCI's share of comprehensive income, (3) dividends paid to NCI, (4) changes from business combinations or NCI transactions, and (5) ending NCI balance. This shows the reconciliation of both parent equity and NCI, providing transparency into ownership interest changes.

quiz.question: A parent sells equipment with book value of $80K to an 80%-owned subsidiary for $120K. The subsidiary depreciates it over 4 years. What is the consolidated adjustment in Year 2?
options: DR: Accumulated Depreciation $10K; CR: Depreciation Expense $10K
DR: Equipment $40K; CR: Gain on Sale $40K
DR: Accumulated Depreciation $10K; CR: Depreciation Expense $10K, AND DR: Retained Earnings $30K; CR: Equipment $40K, Accumulated Depreciation $10K
No adjustment needed in Year 2
quiz.explanation: Downstream intercompany equipment sale requires two adjustments: (1) Eliminate unrealized gain from prior year (now in Retained Earnings): DR: Retained Earnings $40K; CR: Equipment $40K. (2) Eliminate excess depreciation from prior year: DR: Accumulated Depreciation $10K; CR: Retained Earnings $10K. (3) Current year depreciation adjustment: DR: Accumulated Depreciation $10K; CR: Depreciation Expense $10K. Net Year 2 beginning adjustment: DR: Retained Earnings $30K, Equipment $40K; CR: Accumulated Depreciation $10K. Plus current year: DR: Accum. Depr. $10K; CR: Depr. Exp. $10K.

quiz.question: A VIE analysis requires evaluation of which two factors to determine the primary beneficiary?
options: Majority voting rights and equity investment percentage
Power to direct significant activities and obligation to absorb losses/benefits
Debt-to-equity ratio and operational control
Financial statement consolidation preference and tax status
quiz.explanation: ASC 810-10-25-38A requires the primary beneficiary determination to be based on: (1) The power to direct the activities that most significantly impact the VIE's economic performance, AND (2) The obligation to absorb losses or the right to receive benefits that could potentially be significant to the VIE. BOTH conditions must be met. This is fundamentally different from the voting interest model which focuses solely on voting control (>50%).

weeks.title: Week 2: Joint Ventures and Partnership Accounting
weeks.lessonHtml:
Week 2: Joint Ventures and Partnership Accounting

Learning Objectives

  • Understand different types of joint venture structures in construction (corporate JV, partnership, LLC)
  • Master partnership formation accounting and capital contribution valuation
  • Apply profit and loss allocation methods based on partnership agreements
  • Account for partner capital accounts using capital and drawing account systems
  • Handle guaranteed payments, special allocations, and disproportionate distributions
  • Record partnership dissolution, retirement, and admission of new partners
  • Apply equity method accounting for joint venture investments
  • Understand construction industry-specific joint venture arrangements

Section 1: Joint Venture Structures in Construction

1.1 Why Construction Companies Form Joint Ventures

Construction joint ventures (JVs) are partnership arrangements between two or more contractors to bid on and complete a specific project or series of projects. They are particularly common for:

  • Large-scale projects: $50M+ projects requiring combined bonding capacity, equipment, and expertise
  • Specialized work: Combining a general contractor's management with a specialty contractor's technical expertise
  • Geographic expansion: Partnering with local contractors in new markets to leverage relationships and knowledge
  • Risk sharing: Distributing the financial and performance risks of large, complex projects
  • Bonding capacity: Combining surety bond capacity to qualify for projects neither partner could bond individually
CFO Insight: Joint ventures are simultaneously one of construction's most powerful growth tools and most dangerous pitfalls. A well-structured JV can win projects and build capacity you couldn't achieve alone. A poorly structured JV can drain cash, create disputes, and generate liability far exceeding the project's profit. The accounting structure and partnership agreement must align perfectly with the business arrangement.

1.2 Legal Structures for Construction Joint Ventures

Structure Formation Liability Tax Treatment When Used
General Partnership Simple agreement, no state filing Joint and several (unlimited) Pass-through (K-1s) Short-term projects, trusted partners
Limited Liability Company (LLC) State filing required Limited to investment Pass-through or corporate Most common for project JVs
Corporate JV Corporate formation, most complex Limited (corporate veil) Corporate (double taxation unless S-corp) Ongoing JVs, international partners
Equity Joint Venture One partner as general contractor, other as investor GP: unlimited, LP: limited Pass-through Developer-contractor arrangements
Consortium/Teaming Agreement Contract only, no legal entity Defined in contract Each partner reports separately Design-build, government contracts

Accounting Implication: LLC and partnership structures typically use equity method accounting on each partner's books, while corporate JVs may require consolidation if one partner has control.

1.3 Joint Venture Agreement - Critical Accounting Terms

The JV agreement dictates the accounting treatment. Key provisions CFOs must analyze:

  • Ownership percentage: Determines profit/loss allocation and equity method investment percentage
  • Capital contribution requirements: Cash, equipment, bonding capacity - must be valued accurately
  • Profit and loss allocation: May differ from ownership % (e.g., 50/50 ownership but 60/40 profit split)
  • Cash distribution waterfall: Return of capital first? Preferred returns? Profit splits?
  • Voting and control: Determines if one partner consolidates or all use equity method
  • Management fees and reimbursables: One partner may charge JV for project management services
  • Guaranteed payments: Fixed payments to partners regardless of profitability
  • Deficit restoration obligations: Are partners required to fund losses?

Example 1: LLC Joint Venture Formation - Metro Stadium Project

Background: Summit Construction (60% partner) and Valley Contractors (40% partner) form Metro Stadium JV, LLC to build a $200M stadium. The JV agreement calls for:

  • Initial capital contribution: Summit $3M cash + $2M equipment, Valley $3M cash
  • Profit/loss allocation: 60% Summit, 40% Valley
  • Summit provides project management for 3% fee on costs
  • Equipment depreciation charged to JV at fair rental value

Equipment Valuation Issue: Summit's equipment has book value of $1.2M but fair market value of $2M. How should this be handled?

Solution - JV Books (Metro Stadium JV, LLC):

// Initial capital contributions
DR: Cash                           $6,000,000
DR: Equipment                      $2,000,000
    CR: Summit Capital Account                  $5,000,000
    CR: Valley Capital Account                  $3,000,000

// Record equipment at FMV, creating capital accounts reflecting actual contributions

Solution - Summit's Books:

// Record investment in JV
DR: Investment in Metro Stadium JV    $5,000,000
    CR: Cash                                      $3,000,000
    CR: Equipment (at book value)                 $1,200,000
    CR: Gain on Contribution of Equipment           $800,000

// Summit recognizes gain on appreciated property contributed
// Taxable event - equipment contribution treated as sale for tax purposes

Solution - Valley's Books:

// Record investment in JV
DR: Investment in Metro Stadium JV    $3,000,000
    CR: Cash                                      $3,000,000

Key Accounting Issues:

  • JV records all assets at fair value (equipment at $2M)
  • Summit recognizes $800K gain on contribution (FMV $2M - Book value $1.2M)
  • Capital accounts reflect economic contribution: Summit $5M (62.5%), Valley $3M (37.5%)
  • Profit allocation (60/40) differs from capital account % (62.5%/37.5%) - this creates complexity in tax allocations

Section 2: Partnership Capital Accounting

2.1 Partner Capital Account System

Partnership accounting maintains separate capital accounts for each partner to track:

  1. Initial contributions: Cash, property, services contributed
  2. Allocated income/loss: Each partner's share per the agreement
  3. Drawings/distributions: Cash withdrawn by partners
  4. Additional contributions: If partners add capital

Two-Account System (Most Common in Construction):

  • Capital Account: Permanent account showing cumulative equity position
  • Drawing Account: Temporary account for withdrawals, closed to capital at year-end

Typical Capital Account Structure:

Transaction Debit Credit
Initial contribution (cash) Cash Partner Capital
Initial contribution (property) Asset (at FMV) Partner Capital
Allocate net income Income Summary Partner Capital
Allocate net loss Partner Capital Income Summary
Partner withdrawal Partner Drawing Cash
Close drawing to capital (year-end) Partner Capital Partner Drawing

2.2 Profit and Loss Allocation Methods

Construction JV agreements use various P&L allocation methods:

Method 1: Fixed Ratio (Most Common)

Partners share profits and losses in a stated ratio (e.g., 60/40, 70/30). Simple and clear.

Example 2: Fixed Ratio Allocation

Bridge Builders JV has three partners: Alpha (50%), Beta (30%), Gamma (20%). Year 1 net income is $2,000,000.

// Allocation entry
DR: Income Summary                 $2,000,000
    CR: Alpha, Capital                         $1,000,000  (50%)
    CR: Beta, Capital                            $600,000  (30%)
    CR: Gamma, Capital                           $400,000  (20%)

If Year 2 shows a net loss of $500,000:

// Loss allocation entry
DR: Alpha, Capital                   $250,000  (50%)
DR: Beta, Capital                    $150,000  (30%)
DR: Gamma, Capital                   $100,000  (20%)
    CR: Income Summary                           $500,000

Method 2: Salary and Interest Allowances, Then Ratio

Common when partners have different roles (e.g., one manages projects, others provide capital).

Allocation Steps:

  1. Allocate salary allowances to working partners
  2. Allocate interest on capital balances (typically 6-10%)
  3. Allocate remaining profit (or total loss if #1+#2 exceed income) by fixed ratio

Example 3: Salary and Interest Allocation

Partnership Agreement - Skyline Builders JV:

  • Partner Mason (60% ownership): Salary allowance $200K, 8% interest on capital
  • Partner Taylor (40% ownership): No salary, 8% interest on capital
  • Remaining profit/loss: 60/40 ratio
  • Beginning capital balances: Mason $1M, Taylor $1.5M
  • Year 1 net income: $500,000

Allocation Calculation:

Item Mason Taylor Total
Net Income to Allocate $500,000
Step 1: Salary Allowances $200,000 $0 ($200,000)
Step 2: Interest on Capital (8%) $80,000 $120,000 ($200,000)
Remaining to Allocate $100,000
Step 3: Remaining by Ratio (60/40) $60,000 $40,000 ($100,000)
Total Allocation $340,000 $160,000 $500,000 
// Income allocation entry
DR: Income Summary                   $500,000
    CR: Mason, Capital                           $340,000
    CR: Taylor, Capital                          $160,000

Note: Even though Mason has 60% ownership, he receives 68% of profit ($340K ÷ $500K) due to salary and his active role. This compensates for his project management work.

Method 3: Layered/Waterfall Allocation

Sophisticated JVs (especially with financial investors) use waterfall structures:

  1. Return of capital: Distributions first return partners' invested capital
  2. Preferred return: Pay investor partner (e.g., 12% annual return) before others
  3. Catch-up: Operating partner receives profit until reaching same % return as investor
  4. Carried interest: Remaining profits split (e.g., 80/20 to investor/operator)

Example 4: Waterfall Allocation - Development JV

Agreement: Investor contributes $10M (80%), Developer contributes $2M + expertise (20%).

Waterfall Structure:

  1. Return of capital: 100% to partners in proportion to contributions ($10M / $2M = 80/20)
  2. Preferred return: 12% annual return to Investor on unreturned capital
  3. Catch-up: Developer receives 100% until achieving 12% return on their capital
  4. Carried interest: Remaining profit splits 70% Investor / 30% Developer

Year 1 Results: Project generates $15M total cash available for distribution.

Waterfall Tier Amount Investor Developer Cumulative Distribution
1. Return of Capital $12M $10M $2M Inv: $10M, Dev: $2M
2. Preferred Return (12%) $1.2M $1.2M $0 Inv: $11.2M, Dev: $2M
3. Catch-up to Developer $240K $0 $240K Inv: $11.2M, Dev: $2.24M
4. Remaining Split 70/30 $1.56M $1.092M $468K Inv: $12.292M, Dev: $2.708M
TOTAL $15M $12.292M $2.708M 82% / 18%

Accounting Entry - JV Books:

// Distribution based on waterfall
DR: Investor, Capital              $12,292,000
DR: Developer, Capital              $2,708,000
    CR: Cash                                    $15,000,000

Key Point: Developer receives 18% of total distribution despite 20% ownership because they haven't yet achieved their preferred return. Future distributions will shift more toward the Developer as the catch-up tier continues.

2.3 Guaranteed Payments to Partners

Guaranteed payments are amounts paid to partners for services or use of capital, determined without regard to partnership income. Common in construction JVs where one partner provides project management.

Tax Treatment: Guaranteed payments are:

  • Deductible by the partnership (reduces partnership income before allocation)
  • Ordinary income to the partner (reported on Schedule K-1 as guaranteed payment, not distributive share)
  • Subject to self-employment tax for the receiving partner

Example 5: Guaranteed Payments for Project Management

JV Agreement: Coastal Construction (51%) and Mountain Builders (49%) form a JV for a bridge project. Coastal provides project management and receives $300K guaranteed payment regardless of project profitability. Remaining profit/loss splits 51/49.

Year 1 Results: JV generates $2,000,000 revenue, $1,500,000 costs.

Income Calculation:

Item Amount
Revenue $2,000,000
Costs ($1,500,000)
Net income before guaranteed payment $500,000
Guaranteed payment to Coastal ($300,000)
Net income for allocation $200,000

JV Books:

// Record guaranteed payment (monthly accrual, $25K/month)
DR: Guaranteed Payment Expense - Coastal    $300,000
    CR: Cash (or Payable to Coastal)                    $300,000

// Allocate remaining income
DR: Income Summary                          $200,000
    CR: Coastal, Capital                                $102,000  (51%)
    CR: Mountain, Capital                                $98,000  (49%)

Coastal's Total Income from JV:

  • Guaranteed payment: $300,000 (ordinary income, self-employment tax applies)
  • Distributive share: $102,000 (partnership income)
  • Total: $402,000

Coastal's Books (Equity Method):

// Record guaranteed payment received
DR: Cash                                    $300,000
    CR: Equity in JV Earnings                           $300,000

// Record equity in remaining income
DR: Investment in JV                        $102,000
    CR: Equity in JV Earnings                           $102,000

// Net effect: Coastal recognizes $402K total income

Section 3: Partnership Changes - Admission, Withdrawal, and Dissolution

3.1 Admission of a New Partner

A new partner can be admitted through:

  1. Purchase of existing interest: New partner buys out existing partner (transaction between partners, not with partnership)
  2. Investment in partnership: New partner contributes assets to the partnership (increases partnership assets and capital)

Method 1: Purchase of Existing Interest

Example 6: Purchase of Existing Partnership Interest

Background: Highway Builders JV has two partners: Adams (60%, capital balance $600K) and Baker (40%, capital balance $400K). Carter agrees to purchase half of Adams' interest for $400K.

Analysis: Carter pays Adams $400K for 30% interest (half of Adams' 60%). The partnership receives no cash - this is a transaction between Adams and Carter.

Partnership Books:

// Transfer half of Adams' capital to Carter
DR: Adams, Capital                     $300,000
    CR: Carter, Capital                            $300,000

// Note: The $400K paid by Carter to Adams is NOT recorded by the partnership
// Total partnership capital remains $1,000,000

Result:

  • Adams: 30% ownership, $300K capital balance
  • Baker: 40% ownership, $400K capital balance (unchanged)
  • Carter: 30% ownership, $300K capital balance
  • Total capital: $1,000,000 (unchanged)

Adams' Books (personal transaction):

DR: Cash                               $400,000
    CR: Investment in Highway Builders JV              $300,000
    CR: Gain on Sale of Partnership Interest           $100,000

// Adams recognizes $100K gain ($400K sale price - $300K basis)

Method 2: Investment in Partnership with Bonus

When a new partner contributes assets to the partnership, the contribution may reflect:

  • Bonus to existing partners: New partner contributes more than the ownership % received (partnership has value beyond net assets)
  • Bonus to new partner: New partner contributes less than ownership % received (partnership needs capital or new partner brings intangible value)

Example 7: New Partner Investment with Bonus to Existing Partners

Background: Metro Builders JV has two partners with capital balances: Davis $400K (50%) and Evans $400K (50%). Foster invests $300K cash for a 25% interest.

Analysis: Foster contributes $300K but receives only 25% interest. Why would Foster accept this?

  • The JV has goodwill, favorable contracts, or other intangible value
  • Total capital after Foster's contribution: $400K + $400K + $300K = $1,100K
  • Foster's 25% should equal $275K ($1,100K × 25%)
  • Foster contributed $300K but receives $275K equity → $25K bonus to Davis and Evans

Partnership Books:

// Record Foster's investment
DR: Cash                               $300,000
    CR: Davis, Capital                             $12,500  (50% of $25K bonus)
    CR: Evans, Capital                             $12,500  (50% of $25K bonus)
    CR: Foster, Capital                           $275,000

// Alternative presentation showing the bonus calculation:
// Total capital after investment: $1,100,000
// Foster's 25% interest: $275,000
// Foster's investment: $300,000
// Bonus to existing partners: $25,000 (allocated 50/50)

Resulting Capital Balances:

  • Davis: $412,500 (37.5% of $1.1M)
  • Evans: $412,500 (37.5% of $1.1M)
  • Foster: $275,000 (25% of $1.1M)
  • Total: $1,100,000

Example 8: New Partner Investment with Bonus to New Partner

Background: Valley Construction JV (Green $300K / 50% and Hill $300K / 50%) needs an equipment operator with specialized skills. Ivy invests $120K for a 25% interest.

Analysis: Ivy contributes $120K but receives 25% interest. Why?

  • Ivy brings specialized skills critical to project success
  • Total capital after investment: $300K + $300K + $120K = $720K
  • Ivy's 25% should equal $180K ($720K × 25%)
  • Ivy contributed $120K but receives $180K equity → $60K bonus FROM Green and Hill

Partnership Books:

// Record Ivy's investment with bonus
DR: Cash                               $120,000
DR: Green, Capital                      $30,000  (50% of $60K bonus)
DR: Hill, Capital                       $30,000  (50% of $60K bonus)
    CR: Ivy, Capital                              $180,000

Resulting Capital Balances:

  • Green: $270,000 (37.5%)
  • Hill: $270,000 (37.5%)
  • Ivy: $180,000 (25%)
  • Total: $720,000

CFO Note: The bonus method is simpler than the goodwill method (not covered here) because it doesn't require revaluing existing assets or recording intangible assets. The bonus is simply a reallocation of capital among partners.

3.2 Withdrawal and Retirement of a Partner

When a partner leaves, the partnership can:

  1. Pay from partnership assets: Partnership distributes cash/assets to departing partner (reduces total partnership assets)
  2. Sell to remaining partners: Remaining partners personally buy the interest (no effect on partnership assets)
  3. Sell to outside party: New partner admitted through purchase of interest

Example 9: Partner Retirement - Payment Exceeds Capital Balance

Background: Summit Builders JV has three partners: Jones (40%, $400K capital), King (30%, $300K capital), Lee (30%, $300K capital). Jones retires and the partnership pays her $500K for her interest.

Analysis: Jones receives $500K but her capital balance is only $400K. The $100K excess can be treated as:

  • Bonus to Jones from remaining partners (reduces King and Lee's capital), OR
  • Revaluation of partnership assets (records goodwill or asset write-ups)

Method 1: Bonus Method (More Common in Construction)

// Record payment to Jones with bonus
DR: Jones, Capital                     $400,000
DR: King, Capital                       $50,000  (50% of $100K bonus)
DR: Lee, Capital                        $50,000  (50% of $100K bonus)
    CR: Cash                                      $500,000

Resulting Capital Balances:

  • King: $250,000 (50%)
  • Lee: $250,000 (50%)
  • Total: $500,000 (reduced by $500K cash paid to Jones)

Method 2: Goodwill Method (Records Implied Goodwill)

If Jones' 40% interest is worth $500K, then total partnership value is $1,250K ($500K ÷ 40%). Current capital is $1,000K, so implied goodwill is $250K.

// Step 1: Record goodwill
DR: Goodwill                           $250,000
    CR: Jones, Capital                            $100,000  (40%)
    CR: King, Capital                              $75,000  (30%)
    CR: Lee, Capital                               $75,000  (30%)

// Jones' capital now: $400K + $100K = $500K

// Step 2: Pay Jones
DR: Jones, Capital                     $500,000
    CR: Cash                                      $500,000

Resulting Capital Balances:

  • King: $375,000 (50%)
  • Lee: $375,000 (50%)
  • Total: $750,000

CFO Decision: Construction CFOs typically prefer the bonus method because it's simpler and doesn't create intangible assets on the balance sheet that may not have substance. Goodwill method is used when the partnership truly has identifiable value (e.g., long-term contracts, customer relationships).

3.3 Partnership Dissolution and Liquidation

When a construction JV completes its project(s) and dissolves, liquidation follows these steps:

  1. Sell noncash assets (equipment, inventory) and recognize gain/loss
  2. Allocate gain/loss to partners per profit/loss agreement
  3. Pay liabilities to outside creditors
  4. Distribute remaining cash to partners based on capital balances

Key Principle: Partners receive cash equal to their final capital balance, NOT their profit/loss ratio.

Example 10: Partnership Liquidation - Mountain Bridge JV

Pre-Liquidation Balance Sheet:

Assets Liabilities & Capital
Cash $100,000 Accounts Payable $150,000
Equipment (net) $400,000 North, Capital (50%) $200,000
Inventory $50,000 South, Capital (30%) $120,000
West, Capital (20%) $80,000
Total $550,000 Total $550,000

Liquidation Transactions:

Step 1: Sell equipment for $350,000 (loss of $50,000) and inventory for $60,000 (gain of $10,000).

// Sell equipment
DR: Cash                               $350,000
DR: Loss on Sale of Equipment           $50,000
    CR: Equipment                                 $400,000

// Sell inventory
DR: Cash                                $60,000
    CR: Inventory                                  $50,000
    CR: Gain on Sale of Inventory                 $10,000

Step 2: Allocate net loss of $40,000 ($50K loss - $10K gain) to partners.

// Allocate loss per profit/loss ratio (50/30/20)
DR: North, Capital                      $20,000  (50% × $40K)
DR: South, Capital                      $12,000  (30% × $40K)
DR: West, Capital                        $8,000  (20% × $40K)
    CR: Income Summary                            $40,000

Updated Capital Balances:

  • North: $180,000 ($200K - $20K)
  • South: $108,000 ($120K - $12K)
  • West: $72,000 ($80K - $8K)

Step 3: Pay liabilities.

// Pay accounts payable
DR: Accounts Payable                   $150,000
    CR: Cash                                      $150,000

Cash Available for Distribution: $100K + $350K + $60K - $150K = $360K

Step 4: Distribute cash to partners based on capital balances.

// Final distribution
DR: North, Capital                     $180,000
DR: South, Capital                     $108,000
DR: West, Capital                       $72,000
    CR: Cash                                      $360,000

Result: All capital accounts are zero, all cash distributed, partnership dissolved.

Important Note: If any partner had a deficit capital balance after the loss allocation, that partner would be required to contribute cash to the partnership to cover the deficit (assuming the partnership agreement includes a deficit restoration obligation).

Section 4: Equity Method Accounting for JV Investments

4.1 When to Use Equity Method vs. Consolidation

Each partner in a construction JV records their investment using one of these methods:

Ownership/Control Accounting Method Financial Statement Impact
0-20% ownership, no influence Cost or Fair Value (ASC 321) Investment shown at cost/FV; dividends are income
20-50% ownership (significant influence) Equity Method (ASC 323) Investment increases by income share, decreases by dividends
>50% ownership or control Consolidation (ASC 810) Combine all assets, liabilities, revenues, expenses; show NCI
50/50 JV or shared control Equity Method (most common) One-line consolidation; no full consolidation

Construction CFO Note: Most construction JVs are structured as 50/50 or with shared control provisions specifically to avoid consolidation. Partners want to use equity method (one-line consolidation) to keep JV debt off their individual balance sheets.

4.2 Equity Method Journal Entries

Under equity method, the investor records:

  1. Initial investment: DR: Investment in JV; CR: Cash (or assets contributed)
  2. Share of JV income: DR: Investment in JV; CR: Equity in JV Earnings
  3. Share of JV loss: DR: Equity in JV Loss; CR: Investment in JV
  4. Dividends/distributions received: DR: Cash; CR: Investment in JV (reduction of investment, NOT income)
  5. Excess depreciation/amortization: Adjust if purchase price > book value of net assets

Example 11: Complete Equity Method Accounting - Two-Year Period

Background: On January 1, Year 1, Pinnacle Construction invests $2M for a 40% interest in Riverside Dam JV. The JV's total equity on that date is $4.5M, so Pinnacle's share of book value is $1.8M (40% × $4.5M). The $200K excess payment ($2M - $1.8M) is attributable to undervalued equipment with 10-year remaining life.

Year 1 Results:

  • JV reports net income of $800,000
  • JV declares and pays dividends of $200,000

Year 2 Results:

  • JV reports net loss of $100,000
  • JV pays no dividends

Pinnacle's Books - Year 1:

// January 1: Record initial investment
DR: Investment in Riverside Dam JV    $2,000,000
    CR: Cash                                      $2,000,000

// December 31: Record share of JV income
DR: Investment in Riverside Dam JV      $320,000
    CR: Equity in Earnings of JV                    $320,000
// Calculation: $800,000 × 40% = $320,000

// December 31: Record excess depreciation
DR: Equity in Earnings of JV             $20,000
    CR: Investment in Riverside Dam JV               $20,000
// Calculation: $200,000 excess ÷ 10 years = $20,000 annual amortization
// Reduces equity income and investment balance

// December 31: Record dividends received

4.3 Intercompany Profit Elimination in Equity Method

When a construction company sells materials, equipment, or services to a JV it accounts for under equity method, intercompany profit must be deferred until realized through:

  • Use of the asset (depreciation)
  • Sale to third party
  • Consumption in a project

Example 12: Intercompany Equipment Sale to Joint Venture

Background: Alpine Construction owns 40% of Summit Bridge JV (equity method). Alpine sells a crane to the JV for $500K. Alpine's cost was $400K, so Alpine records $100K gross profit. The JV depreciates the crane over 5 years (straight-line).

Year 1 - Alpine's Books:

// Record sale to JV
DR: Cash (or Receivable from JV)       $500,000
    CR: Equipment                                 $400,000
    CR: Gain on Sale                              $100,000

// Defer Alpine's share of unrealized gain
DR: Equity in Earnings of JV            $40,000
    CR: Investment in Summit Bridge JV            $40,000
// Calculation: $100,000 gain × 40% ownership = $40,000 to defer
// Only defer investor's proportionate share

// Realize portion through depreciation
DR: Investment in Summit Bridge JV       $8,000
    CR: Equity in Earnings of JV                   $8,000
// Calculation: ($100K gain ÷ 5 years) × 40% = $8,000 realized in Year 1

Net Effect Year 1:

  • Gain on Sale recognized: $100,000
  • Equity method adjustment (deferral): -$40,000
  • Equity method adjustment (realization): +$8,000
  • Net income impact: $100K - $40K + $8K = $68,000
  • Remaining deferred gain: $32,000 (will be realized $8K/year over next 4 years)

Years 2-5: Alpine continues to recognize $8,000 per year as the crane is depreciated by the JV.

// Each year, Years 2-5
DR: Investment in Summit Bridge JV       $8,000
    CR: Equity in Earnings of JV                   $8,000

CFO Insight: This creates a timing difference. Alpine gets $68K income in Year 1, then $8K per year for four more years, for total of $100K over five years - matching the original gain. The equity method essentially forces recognition to match the JV's use of the asset.
