Contract assets represent revenue recognized in excess of amounts billed (unbilled receivables). Contract liabilities represent advance payments and billings in excess of revenue recognized (deferred revenue). During 2024, the Company recognized $23 million of revenue that was included in contract liabilities at the beginning of the year.

Transaction Price Allocated to Remaining Performance Obligations (Backlog)

As of December 31, 2024, the aggregate transaction price allocated to remaining performance obligations (backlog) is $485 million. The Company expects to recognize revenue on these contracts as follows:

  • 2025: $320 million (66%)
  • 2026: $135 million (28%)
  • 2027: $25 million (5%)
  • 2028+: $5 million (1%)

Significant Judgments

The Company uses the cost-to-cost method to measure progress on contracts, which requires estimates of total contract costs. These estimates are subject to change as projects progress and may result in increases or decreases in revenue and profit. During 2024, cumulative catch-up adjustments increased gross profit by $4.2 million.

The Company includes variable consideration (incentive bonuses, change orders) in the transaction price only to the extent it is probable that a significant reversal of revenue will not occur. As of December 31, 2024, the Company has constrained $8.5 million of potential incentive bonuses that are not included in the transaction price due to uncertainty regarding achievement.

Practice Problems

Problem 1: Multiple Performance Obligations with Allocation

Scenario: Apex Construction signs a $6M contract including:

  • Site preparation and demolition (estimated SSP: $600K)
  • New construction (estimated SSP: $5M)
  • Landscaping (estimated SSP: $500K)

Analysis shows:

  • Demolition is distinct (customer could hire specialty demo contractor)
  • Construction is the primary deliverable
  • Landscaping is distinct (performed after construction completion)

Required:

  1. Determine the number of performance obligations.
  2. Allocate the $6M transaction price to each performance obligation.
  3. Prepare revenue recognition entries if demolition completes in Month 2 (costs $480K) and construction is 30% complete at Month 6 (costs $1.5M).

Solution:

1. Performance Obligations: Three distinct obligations

  • Demolition (distinct)
  • Construction (distinct)
  • Landscaping (distinct)

2. Transaction Price Allocation:

Performance Obligation SSP % of Total SSP Allocated Price
Demolition $600,000 9.8% $590,164
Construction $5,000,000 82.0% $4,918,033
Landscaping $500,000 8.2% $491,803
Total $6,100,000 100% $6,000,000

Calculations:

  • Demolition: ($600K / $6,100K) × $6M = $590,164
  • Construction: ($5M / $6,100K) × $6M = $4,918,033
  • Landscaping: ($500K / $6,100K) × $6M = $491,803

3. Revenue Recognition Entries:

// Month 2: Demolition complete
DR: Cost of Revenue - Demolition        $480,000
DR: Accounts Receivable                 $590,164
    CR: Revenue - Demolition                       $590,164
    CR: Cash                                       $480,000
// Gross profit on demolition: $110,164 (18.7% margin)

// Month 6: Construction 30% complete
DR: Cost of Revenue - Construction    $1,500,000
DR: Contract Asset                    $1,475,410
    CR: Revenue - Construction                   $1,475,410
    CR: Cash/Payables                            $1,500,000
// Revenue: 30% × $4,918,033 = $1,475,410
// Gross profit to date: ($1,475,410 - $1,500,000) = LOSS of $24,590
// This suggests project may be over budget

// Landscaping: No revenue yet (not started)

Problem 2: Variable Consideration with Constraint

Scenario: Valley Contractors has a $25M bridge contract with completion bonus structure:

  • Complete 60+ days early: $1.5M bonus
  • Complete 30-59 days early: $750K bonus
  • Complete on time or late: $0 bonus; late penalties $50K/day (max $500K)

At 50% completion, Valley estimates:

  • 20% probability of 70 days early → $1.5M bonus
  • 45% probability of 40 days early → $750K bonus
  • 30% probability of on-time completion → $0
  • 5% probability of 5 days late → $250K penalty

Required:

  1. Calculate the expected value of variable consideration.
  2. Determine what amount, if any, should be included in the transaction price considering the constraint.
  3. Prepare the journal entry to adjust revenue at the 50% completion point if no variable consideration was previously included.

Solution:

1. Expected Value Calculation:

Outcome Amount Probability Expected Value
70 days early $1,500,000 20% $300,000
40 days early $750,000 45% $337,500
On time $0 30% $0
5 days late ($250,000) 5% ($12,500)
Total Expected Value $625,000

2. Amount to Include (Considering Constraint):

Analysis:

  • Expected value: $625,000
  • Most likely outcome: 40 days early ($750K bonus at 45% probability)
  • Combined probability of achieving SOME bonus: 65% (20% + 45%)
  • Probability of NO bonus or penalty: 35% (30% + 5%)

CFO Judgment: It is NOT probable that $625K (or even $750K) will be achieved without significant reversal because:

  • 35% combined probability of $0 or penalty is material
  • Project is only 50% complete (18+ months remaining)
  • Weather, labor, material delays could easily impact schedule

Conservative Approach: Include $0 variable consideration at this point. Wait until project is 75%+ complete and schedule certainty is higher.

Alternative (Moderate) Approach: If Valley has strong track record and project is ahead of schedule, could include $400K-$500K (representing high confidence in at least some bonus).

Recommendation: Include $0 at 50% completion; reassess at 75% completion.

3. Journal Entry:

// No entry at 50% completion since we're not including variable consideration
// Continue recognizing revenue based on $25M base contract price

// Revenue at 50% completion:
DR: Contract Asset                  $12,500,000
    CR: Revenue                                $12,500,000
// 50% × $25M = $12.5M

Problem 3: Contract Modification - Cumulative Catch-Up

Scenario: Through Month 10, Phoenix Builders has recognized:

  • Revenue: $6M (60% × $10M original contract)
  • Costs: $4.8M (60% of $8M estimated total cost)
  • Gross profit: $1.2M

In Month 11, customer approves change order adding $2M scope (not distinct - integrated with remaining work). Additional cost estimate: $1.5M.

Required:

  1. Calculate the revised transaction price and total estimated cost.
  2. Calculate the revised percentage of completion.
  3. Determine the cumulative catch-up adjustment needed.
  4. Prepare the journal entry in Month 11.

Solution:

1. Revised Contract Terms:

Item Original Change Order Revised Total
Contract Price $10,000,000 +$2,000,000 $12,000,000
Estimated Total Cost $8,000,000 +$1,500,000 $9,500,000
Expected Gross Profit $2,000,000 +$500,000 $2,500,000
Gross Profit % 20.0% 25.0% 20.8%

2. Revised % Complete:

  • Costs incurred to date: $4,800,000
  • Revised total estimated cost: $9,500,000
  • Revised % complete: $4.8M / $9.5M = 50.5%

3. Cumulative Catch-Up Adjustment:

Item Amount
Revenue that should be recognized (50.5% × $12M) $6,063,158
Revenue already recognized (through Month 10) ($6,000,000)
Cumulative Catch-Up - Increase Revenue $63,158

4. Journal Entry - Month 11:

// Record change order addition to contract
DR: Contract Asset                   $2,000,000
    CR: Revenue - Change Orders                  $2,000,000

// Record cumulative catch-up adjustment
DR: Contract Asset                      $63,158
    CR: Revenue - Cumulative Adjustment            $63,158

// Net Month 11 revenue impact: $2,000,000 + $63,158 = $2,063,158

// Alternative single entry:
DR: Contract Asset                   $2,063,158
    CR: Revenue                                  $2,063,158

Explanation: The catch-up is POSITIVE because costs incurred ($4.8M) represent a smaller percentage of the new total cost ($9.5M = 50.5%) compared to the old calculation (60%). The project is "less complete" after adding the change order scope, but the cumulative revenue still increases by $63K to properly reflect 50.5% of $12M.

Key Takeaways

CFO Insight: Navigating ASC 606 Complexity

After implementing ASC 606 with dozens of construction companies, here are the critical success factors:

  1. Performance obligation determination is judgment-heavy: Don't assume everything is "one performance obligation" just because it's a construction contract. Carefully evaluate whether demolition, site work, and specialty systems are distinct. The economic consequence is significant - separating obligations accelerates revenue for completed components.
  2. Variable consideration constraint is your friend: ASC 606's constraint prevents premature recognition of uncertain bonuses and change orders. Yes, it delays revenue recognition compared to old rules. But it also prevents embarrassing reversals when bonuses aren't achieved or change orders aren't approved. Better to be conservative.
  3. Document contract modifications contemporaneously: Every change order should be evaluated as Type 1 (separate), Type 2 (prospective), or Type 3 (cumulative catch-up) at the time of modification. Don't wait until year-end close to figure this out - you'll get it wrong without real-time facts.
  4. Principal vs. agent matters more than you think: CMAR vs. CM Agency can represent $50M difference in reported revenue (even if gross profit is similar). This affects bonding capacity, debt covenants, and market perception. Structure your contracts intentionally.
  5. Warranty accounting isn't just for manufacturers: Construction companies have warranty obligations too. Estimate probable costs and accrue consistently. Extended maintenance agreements are separate performance obligations - don't bury them in project revenue.
  6. Disclosure requirements are extensive: ASC 606 requires disaggregated revenue, contract balances, backlog, and significant judgments. Plan for these disclosures during implementation - don't treat them as an afterthought.
  7. Revenue recognized ≠ Cash collected: ASC 606 often accelerates revenue recognition (over time) while billings lag (monthly billing cycles). Monitor contract assets (unbilled receivables) closely - growth in contract assets consumes cash and signals billing issues.
  8. Cumulative catch-up adjustments are normal: As estimates change, cumulative catch-ups (positive or negative) adjust prior period revenue. Disclose significant adjustments separately to show they're estimate changes, not operational issues.
  9. Don't recognize revenue for unapproved change orders: The temptation is strong when you've incurred costs. Resist. ASC 606 requires probable approval of both scope AND price. Treat uncertain change orders as claims - capitalize costs if recoverable, but defer revenue recognition.
  10. Cost-to-cost remains king: Despite all the complexity, the cost-to-cost input method remains the predominant measure of progress for construction. Ensure your project managers understand that EVERY cost decision affects revenue recognition.

Common Pitfalls

  • Bundling everything into "one performance obligation" by default: Many construction companies assume the entire contract is one obligation because "it's all one project." Wrong. Carefully evaluate each promise in the contract to determine if it's distinct.
  • Including variable consideration too aggressively: Incentive bonuses and change orders often fail the "constraint" test (probable that significant reversal won't occur). Be conservative - you can always increase revenue later when certainty improves.
  • Treating all contract modifications as cumulative catch-up: Not all change orders are Type 3 modifications. If the change adds distinct goods/services at standalone prices, it's a separate contract. Failing to identify Type 1 modifications delays revenue recognition.
  • Recognizing gross revenue when acting as agent: Construction managers providing only agency services (owner contracts directly with subs) should recognize NET revenue (fee only), not gross project costs. Incorrectly recognizing gross revenue inflates revenue and violates ASC 606.
  • Failing to allocate discounts proportionately: When contract price is less than sum of standalone selling prices, allocate the discount proportionately across all performance obligations (unless you can prove it relates to one specific obligation).
  • Ignoring warranty obligations: Construction companies often forget to accrue assurance-type warranty costs. Historical experience should guide the accrual percentage (typically 0.3% to 1.0% of contract revenue).
  • Recognizing extended warranty revenue immediately: Service-type warranties (extended maintenance agreements) are separate performance obligations. Don't include them in construction revenue - defer and recognize ratably over the service period.
  • Confusing contract assets and accounts receivable: Contract asset = revenue recognized but not billable yet (unbilled). A/R = billed and collectible. Don't report all revenue as A/R - properly classify based on billing rights.
  • Not reassessing variable consideration quarterly: Variable consideration estimates must be updated each reporting period as facts change. Failing to reassess can result in significant catch-up adjustments at project completion.
  • Inadequate disclosure: ASC 606 disclosures are extensive (disaggregated revenue, contract balances, backlog, significant judgments). Many companies underestimate the effort required. Plan ahead and build systems to capture this data.

Next Week Preview

In Week 4: Real Estate Development Accounting, we'll explore construction accounting for real estate developers:

  • Land development and lot cost allocation: Relative value method, specific identification, and area method
  • Model homes and sales offices: Capitalization, depreciation, and conversion to inventory
  • HOA and common area accounting: Formation, turnover, and cost allocation
  • Percentage of completion for developers: Application to speculative projects
  • Revenue recognition for lot sales: Timing, deposit accounting, and buyer financing contingencies
  • Joint ventures for land development: Developer-investor partnerships and profit-sharing waterfalls

Real estate development combines construction accounting with real estate principles, creating unique challenges for CFOs in this sector.

flashcards.question: What are the two criteria for a good/service to be 'distinct' under ASC 606?
flashcards.answer: (1) Capable of being distinct - customer can benefit from it alone or with readily available resources, AND (2) Distinct within context of contract - promise is separately identifiable (not highly interdependent/integrated with other promises). Both must be met to be a separate performance obligation. Example: Demolition + Construction may be bundled if demolition is preparatory; Demolition + Maintenance are likely distinct.

flashcards.question: How is transaction price allocated when there are multiple performance obligations?
flashcards.answer: Allocate based on relative standalone selling prices (SSP). Calculate each obligation's SSP, sum them, then allocate contract price proportionately. Example: SSPs of $800K, $8.5M, $450K (total $9.75M) for $10M contract: allocate $820K (8.2%), $8,718K (87.2%), $462K (4.6%). Discounts allocated proportionately unless evidence shows discount relates to one specific obligation.

flashcards.question: What is the 'constraint' on variable consideration under ASC 606?
flashcards.answer: Include variable consideration in transaction price ONLY to the extent it's PROBABLE that a significant revenue reversal will NOT occur. Assess likelihood considering: experience with similar contracts, number of possible outcomes, time until resolution, susceptibility to outside factors. More restrictive than old 'reasonably assured' standard - be conservative with bonuses and change orders.

flashcards.question: What are the two methods for estimating variable consideration?
flashcards.answer: (1) Expected value - probability-weighted amount (use when many possible outcomes). Example: 30% × $800K + 50% × $400K + 20% × $0 = $440K. (2) Most likely amount - single most likely outcome (use when binary: achieve or not). Example: 70% probability of $600K LD → use $600K. Choose the method that better predicts the amount of consideration.

flashcards.question: What are the three types of contract modifications under ASC 606?
flashcards.answer: Type 1 (Separate Contract): Adds distinct goods/services at SSP → account as new contract. Type 2 (Prospective): Remaining goods/services distinct → terminate old, start new (no catch-up). Type 3 (Cumulative Catch-Up): Remaining goods/services NOT distinct → modify existing contract retrospectively (cumulative adjustment to revenue). Most construction change orders are Type 3.

flashcards.question: How does cumulative catch-up accounting work for contract modifications?
flashcards.answer: Type 3 modifications adjust the entire contract retrospectively. Calculate: (1) Revised % complete using costs incurred ÷ new total cost, (2) Revenue that should have been recognized (revised % × new total price), (3) Less revenue already recognized, (4) Difference = catch-up (positive or negative). Example: 43% × $9.8M = $4,214K; already recognized $4,250K → catch-up of ($36K) reduction.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between principal and agent under ASC 606?
flashcards.answer: Principal: Controls good/service before transfer → recognize GROSS revenue (include sub costs in revenue and COGS). Agent: Arranges for another party to provide → recognize NET revenue (fee/commission only). Principal indicators: primarily responsible for fulfillment, inventory risk, pricing discretion, integrates services. CMAR is principal; CM Agency is agent.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between assurance-type and service-type warranties?
flashcards.answer: Assurance-type: Assures product complies with specifications → accrue warranty liability (not separate performance obligation). Service-type: Provides service BEYOND assurance → separate performance obligation (allocate transaction price, recognize over service period). Service-type indicators: customer can purchase separately, extends beyond standard period, covers customer acts or abnormal damage.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between contract assets and accounts receivable?
flashcards.answer: Contract asset: Revenue recognized but not yet billable (unbilled receivables). Unconditional right hasn't been established. A/R: Billed and collectible (unconditional right to payment). When billing occurs: DR: A/R; CR: Contract Asset. Both are current assets. Contract liabilities (deferred revenue) = cash received before revenue recognition (advance payments, billings in excess).

flashcards.question: What are the key ASC 606 disclosure requirements?
flashcards.answer: (1) Disaggregated revenue by market/contract type, (2) Contract balances (contract assets, A/R, contract liabilities) with reconciliation, (3) Performance obligations and timing, (4) Transaction price allocated to remaining performance obligations (backlog) with expected timing, (5) Significant judgments (methods, estimates, constraints). Extensive disclosures - plan ahead and build systems to capture data.

quiz.question: Under ASC 606, a good or service is 'distinct' and represents a separate performance obligation if:
options: The customer could benefit from it on its own
The customer could benefit from it on its own AND it's separately identifiable from other promises
It's billed separately from other services
It has a standalone selling price
quiz.explanation: ASC 606-10-25-14 requires BOTH criteria: (1) Capable of being distinct - customer can benefit from it alone or with readily available resources, AND (2) Distinct within context of contract - separately identifiable from other promises (not highly interdependent/integrated). Both must be met for a separate performance obligation.

quiz.question: A $10M contract includes demolition (SSP $800K), construction (SSP $8.5M), and maintenance (SSP $450K). Total SSP is $9.75M. What is the allocated price for construction?
quiz.explanation: Transaction price is allocated based on relative standalone selling prices. Construction allocation = ($8.5M / $9.75M) × $10M = 87.18% × $10M = $8,717,949. The $250K discount ($10M contract vs. $9.75M total SSP) is allocated proportionately across all three performance obligations unless evidence shows it relates to only one.

quiz.question: Variable consideration should be included in the transaction price:
options: Always, using the expected value method
Only when certain (100% probability)
To the extent it's probable that a significant reversal will NOT occur
Only when the customer agrees in writing
quiz.explanation: ASC 606-10-32-11 requires including variable consideration only when it's PROBABLE (high likelihood) that a significant revenue reversal will not occur. This 'constraint' is more restrictive than prior guidance. Companies must assess likelihood of reversal considering factors like: experience with similar contracts, number of possible outcomes, time until resolution, and susceptibility to factors outside company's control.

quiz.question: Alpine Construction has a contract with early completion bonus: 30+ days early = $800K, 15-29 days early = $400K, on time = $0. At 60% complete, probabilities are 30%/50%/20% respectively. What amount should likely be included in the transaction price?
options: $800,000 (maximum possible)
$400,000 (most likely outcome, applying constraint)
$0 (too uncertain)
quiz.explanation: Expected value = $440K, but the constraint requires assessing if this amount is probable without significant reversal. The most likely outcome is $400K (50% probability), and combined probability of achieving SOME bonus is 80%. A conservative approach includes $400K (the middle scenario) rather than full expected value, as there's still 20% probability of $0 and project uncertainty remains.

quiz.question: A contract with liquidated damages of $50K/day for late completion, capped at $1M. At 92% complete, there's 70% probability of 12-day delay ($600K LD). The most likely amount method suggests reducing transaction price by:
options: $0 - wait until completion
$600,000 (most likely outcome)
$1,000,000 (maximum exposure)
$420,000 (70% × $600K expected value)
quiz.explanation: When late completion is the most likely outcome (70% probability) and project is substantially complete (92%), it's probable the company will incur the LD. Use the 'most likely amount' method (single most likely outcome) rather than expected value. Reduce transaction price by $600K to reflect the most likely LD. Failing to do so would result in revenue reversal at completion.

quiz.question: At Month 8, a $8M construction contract (53.1% complete, $4.25M revenue recognized) is modified by a $1.8M change order for integrated additional scope. After modification, total costs are $7.9M and costs incurred are $3.4M. What is the cumulative catch-up adjustment?
options: $1,800,000 increase
$1,764,000 increase
($36,000) decrease
$0 - prospective only
quiz.explanation: This is a Type 3 modification (not distinct). New total: $9.8M revenue, $7.9M cost. Revised % complete: $3.4M ÷ $7.9M = 43.0%. Revenue should be: 43.0% × $9.8M = $4,214K. Already recognized: $4,250K. Cumulative catch-up: $4,214K - $4,250K = ($36K) DECREASE. The project is now less complete (43% vs. 53%) because costs incurred represent a smaller percentage of the larger total cost base.

quiz.question: Which contract modification should be accounted for as a SEPARATE contract (Type 1)?
options: Change order adding scope integrated with remaining work
Change order adding distinct scope at standalone selling price
Customer-directed acceleration of existing scope
Reduction in contract scope with price adjustment
quiz.explanation: Type 1 modifications are separate contracts when: (1) the modification adds distinct goods/services, AND (2) the price increase reflects standalone selling prices for the additional goods/services. Example: Adding a separate parking garage to an office building project at market rates. Type 2 (prospective) and Type 3 (cumulative catch-up) apply when goods/services are NOT distinct or not priced at SSP.

quiz.question: Under ASC 606, a construction company is a PRINCIPAL (recognizes gross revenue) rather than AGENT when:
options: The company contracts directly with all subcontractors and is primarily responsible for fulfillment
The company provides only project management services
The owner contracts directly with subcontractors
The company charges a fixed fee regardless of project costs
quiz.explanation: ASC 606-10-55-37 indicators of principal status: (1) primarily responsible for fulfilling the promise, (2) has inventory risk, (3) has discretion in setting prices, (4) integrates goods/services into combined output. Construction Manager at Risk (CMAR) is principal - recognizes gross revenue including subcontractor costs. Construction Manager Agent (CM Agency) recognizes only the management fee (net revenue).

quiz.question: What is the key difference between assurance-type and service-type warranties?
options: Length of warranty period
Assurance-type assures compliance; service-type provides additional service beyond compliance
Cost to the customer
Assurance-type is required; service-type is optional
quiz.explanation: ASC 606-10-55-31: Assurance-type warranty assures the product complies with agreed specifications (accrue as warranty liability, not separate performance obligation). Service-type warranty provides a service in addition to assurance of compliance (separate performance obligation, allocate transaction price). Service-type indicators: customer can purchase separately, extends beyond standard period, covers acts of customer or damage beyond normal use.

quiz.question: A $10M project includes a 1-year standard warranty (estimated cost $50K) and optional 3-year extended maintenance ($180K). How should these be accounted for?
options: Both are separate performance obligations
Standard warranty: accrue $50K liability; Extended maintenance: separate performance obligation, defer $180K
Both combined into single $230K accrual
No accounting needed until warranty claims occur
quiz.explanation: Standard warranty is assurance-type (assures construction quality): DR: Warranty Expense $50K; CR: Warranty Liability $50K. Extended maintenance is service-type (optional, provides service beyond assurance): Allocate $180K as separate performance obligation, recognize ratably over 3 years ($5K/month). At completion, balance sheet shows: Warranty Liability $50K (reduced as claims occur) and Deferred Revenue $180K (reduced as maintenance services provided).

quiz.question: Under ASC 606-10-50, which of the following disclosures is NOT required?
options: Disaggregated revenue by market sector or contract type
Contract balances (contract assets, receivables, liabilities)
Transaction price allocated to remaining performance obligations (backlog)
Individual customer names and contract values for all projects >$10M
quiz.explanation: ASC 606-10-50 requires: (1) disaggregated revenue, (2) contract balances with reconciliation, (3) performance obligations and timing, (4) transaction price allocated to remaining performance obligations (backlog), and (5) significant judgments. Individual customer information and specific contract values are NOT required disclosures (and may violate customer confidentiality). Aggregate backlog by year is required.

quiz.question: A company recognizes $12.5M revenue (50% × $25M) through Month 10. In Month 11, cumulative catch-up adjustments increase gross profit by $400K due to cost reductions. What is the Month 11 revenue impact?
options: $400,000 (the catch-up adjustment)
Depends on whether catch-up is from cost changes or price changes
$0 - cumulative catch-ups don't affect revenue, only gross profit
quiz.explanation: The impact depends on WHY gross profit increased. If from COST reductions (e.g., expected total cost decreased from $20M to $19M): Revenue unchanged at $12.5M, costs reduced, profit increases $500K (50% of $1M cost reduction). If from PRICE increases (e.g., change order): Revenue increases. Cumulative catch-ups can result from estimate changes (costs), contract modifications (price), or both. The $400K profit increase likely involves BOTH revenue and cost adjustments.

quiz.question: When should revenue be recognized for an unapproved change order where scope is accepted but price is still being negotiated?
options: Immediately, using expected cost + reasonable margin
When the customer verbally agrees to pay
When it's probable the customer will approve the price and the amount can be reliably estimated
Only when the change order is fully executed
quiz.explanation: ASC 606 guidance on contract modifications: Unapproved change orders can be included in transaction price if: (1) parties approved scope change, (2) it's PROBABLE parties will approve price, and (3) amount can be estimated reliably without significant reversal. This is more restrictive than old 'reasonably assured' standard. Many companies defer revenue recognition until written approval, capitalizing costs as contract asset if recoverable.

quiz.question: Contract assets vs. accounts receivable - what is the primary distinction?
options: Contract assets are long-term; A/R is current
Contract assets = revenue recognized but not billable yet (unbilled); A/R = billed and collectible
Contract assets include retainage; A/R does not
Contract assets are net of contract liabilities; A/R is gross
quiz.explanation: ASC 606-10-45-1: Contract asset represents the right to consideration for goods/services transferred but not yet billable (unbilled receivables/work in progress). Accounts receivable represents unconditional right to payment (already billed or billable). When company bills a contract asset, reclassify: DR: A/R; CR: Contract Asset. Both are typically current assets. Retainage can be either contract asset or A/R depending on billing status.

quiz.question: Which method is used MOST commonly for measuring progress toward completion in construction contracts?
options: Units delivered or produced
Cost-to-cost input method
Surveys of work performed
Time elapsed
quiz.explanation: ASC 606-10-55-21: The cost-to-cost method (costs incurred ÷ estimated total costs) is the predominant measure of progress for construction contracts recognized over time. It provides an objective, faithful depiction of progress toward satisfaction of performance obligations. Alternative input methods (labor hours, machine hours) or output methods (surveys, milestones) may be used when cost-to-cost doesn't depict progress, but this is rare in construction.

weeks.title: Week 4: Real Estate Development Accounting
weeks.lessonHtml:
Week 4: Real Estate Development Accounting

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the unique accounting challenges for construction companies engaged in real estate development
  • Apply land development cost accounting and lot cost allocation methods
  • Account for model homes, sales offices, and amenities
  • Navigate homeowners association (HOA) formation, operation, and turnover accounting
  • Apply percentage of completion method to speculative construction (inventory vs. contract accounting)
  • Recognize revenue for lot sales under ASC 606
  • Account for developer-investor joint ventures with profit-sharing waterfalls
  • Apply relative value, specific identification, and area methods for cost allocation

Section 1: Land Development Cost Accounting

1.1 Real Estate Development vs. Construction Contracting

Construction companies that enter real estate development face fundamentally different accounting compared to traditional contracting:

Aspect Construction Contractor Real Estate Developer
Accounting Model Contract accounting (ASC 606) Inventory accounting (ASC 360) + ASC 606 for sales
Revenue Recognition Over time (% completion) At point of sale (when control transfers)
Balance Sheet Classification Contract assets/liabilities Real estate inventory (current asset)
Cost Capitalization Job costing by contract Land, development, construction costs by project/lot
Risk Profile Performance risk (deliver per contract) Market risk (sell at projected prices)

CFO Insight: Many construction companies mistakenly apply contract accounting (% completion revenue recognition) to speculative development projects. This is wrong. Real estate held for sale is INVENTORY, not a contract asset. Revenue is recognized when lots/homes are SOLD, not as they're developed or built. This dramatically changes cash flow management, financial covenants, and tax planning.

1.2 Capitalizable Land Development Costs

Under ASC 970-360-25, real estate developers capitalize ALL costs directly related to acquiring and developing land:

Acquisition Costs:

  • Purchase price of raw land
  • Closing costs, title insurance, legal fees
  • Due diligence costs (surveys, environmental studies, geotechnical reports)
  • Earnest money deposits and option payments

Pre-Development Costs:

  • Master planning and engineering design
  • Entitlement and permitting fees
  • Zoning and land use approvals
  • Impact fees and development assessments
  • Environmental remediation required for development

Development Costs:

  • Site clearing, grading, and earthwork
  • Streets, curbs, gutters, sidewalks
  • Utilities (water, sewer, electric, gas)
  • Storm drainage and retention ponds
  • Landscaping and common area improvements
  • Model homes and sales office (if directly related)
  • Interest on construction loans during development (capitalized)

NOT Capitalizable (Expense as Incurred):

  • General and administrative overhead (unless directly traceable)
  • Marketing and advertising (after sales begin)
  • Selling commissions and closing costs
  • Interest after development is substantially complete

1.3 Interest Capitalization During Development

ASC 835-20 requires capitalizing interest on funds borrowed to finance real estate development. Interest capitalization begins when:

  1. Expenditures have been made
  2. Activities necessary to prepare asset for intended use are in progress
  3. Interest cost is being incurred

Interest capitalization STOPS when the asset is substantially complete and ready for intended use (i.e., lots are ready for sale/building).

Section 2: Lot Cost Allocation Methods

2.1 Three Allocation Methods

When a developer acquires and develops land with multiple lots/units, total costs must be allocated to individual lots. Three methods are acceptable:

  1. Relative Value Method: Allocate based on relative sales values (most common)
  2. Specific Identification Method: Allocate specific traceable costs (for significantly different lots)
  3. Area Method: Allocate based on lot size (square footage or acreage)

Method 1: Relative Value Method

Allocate total cost in proportion to estimated sales values of individual lots. This is the MOST COMMON method because it best reflects the economics - premium lots (better views, larger size, preferred location) should bear higher costs.

Formula: Lot Cost = (Lot Sales Value ÷ Total Sales Values) × Total Cost

3.1 Accounting Treatment

4.1 HOA Formation and Developer Responsibility

Real estate developers typically form HOAs to maintain common areas (parks, pools, entry monuments) and enforce covenants. The developer initially controls the HOA until turnover to homeowners (typically when 75-90% of lots/homes are sold).

Section 5: Revenue Recognition for Lot and Home Sales

5.1 ASC 606 Application to Real Estate Sales

Under ASC 606-10-55-8, revenue from real estate sales is typically recognized at the point in time when control transfers to the buyer, usually at closing. However, buyers may have significant continuing involvement that delays revenue recognition.

Indicators of Control Transfer (Revenue Recognition):

  1. Closing has occurred (title transferred)
  2. Buyer has paid adequate initial investment (typically 10-25% of sales price)
  3. Buyer's receivable is not subject to subordination
  4. Seller has transferred possession
  5. Seller has no continuing involvement (e.g., no obligation to construct home)
CFO Insight - Lot Sales vs. Home Sales:

Many developers make a critical error: recognizing revenue on lot sales when the buyer (a homebuilder) is not creditworthy or the sale is contingent on the builder's ability to sell homes.

Lot Sale (Clean Sale): Developer sells finished lot to creditworthy homebuilder for cash or with seller financing (10-20% down). Control transfers, recognize revenue immediately.

Lot Sale (Contingent): Developer "sells" lot to builder who hasn't paid, with understanding developer will buy back if builder can't sell homes. This is NOT a sale - control hasn't transferred. Treat as deposit, don't recognize revenue until contingencies resolve.

The distinction is critical for financial reporting, debt covenants, and tax planning. Aggressive developers recognize revenue prematurely, creating phantom profit and tax liability with no cash.

Section 6: Developer-Investor Joint Ventures

6.1 Typical Structure

Real estate development often involves partnerships between:

  • Developer: Provides expertise, management, entitlements (typically 10-30% equity)
  • Investor: Provides capital (typically 70-90% equity)

Profit is typically split via waterfall structure designed to:

  1. Return investor's capital first
  2. Pay investor preferred return (8-15% annual return)
  3. Give developer "catch-up" to equalize returns
  4. Split remaining profit (typically 70% investor / 30% developer as "promoted interest")

Example 8: Developer-Investor JV with Waterfall - Canyon Ridge Development

  2. Preferred return: 12% annual return to Investor on unreturned capital
  3. Catch-up: Developer receives 100% until achieving 12% return
  4. Promoted interest: Remaining profit 70% Investor / 30% Developer

Key Takeaways

CFO Insight: Real Estate Development - The Good, The Bad, The Ugly

The Good: Real estate development offers construction companies:

  • Higher profit margins (20-40% vs. 5-15% for contracting)
  • Control over project selection and timing
  • Appreciation on land holdings
  • Vertical integration (self-perform construction)

The Bad: Real estate development is fundamentally different from contracting:

  • Market risk: You're betting on future sales prices and absorption rates
  • Capital intensive: No progress billings - all cash invested upfront
  • Long cycle time: 3-7 years from land acquisition to final home sale
  • No revenue until sale: Inventory accounting (not % completion) means no P&L impact until you sell

The Ugly: Where contractors fail in development:

  1. Cash flow ignorance: Contractors are used to billing monthly and collecting cash. Development ties up $5M+ with ZERO revenue for 2-3 years. Then sales may be slow. Cash crunches kill developers.
  2. Market timing disasters: Starting development in 2006-2007 destroyed hundreds of contractors-turned-developers in 2008-2009. You're "all in" with no ability to walk away once you've spent $10M on infrastructure.
  3. Accounting mistakes: Contractors mistakenly apply % completion to inventory, recognizing "revenue" as lots are developed. This is WRONG. Creates phantom profit, accelerates tax, and violates GAAP.
  4. Undercapitalized partnerships: Contractors contribute land or expertise valued at $2M for 40% ownership, while investor contributes $8M cash for 60%. When project needs another $3M, contractor can't fund their 40% ($1.2M), leading to dilution or project failure.
  5. Waterfall misunderstandings: Contractors expect "40% of profit" but waterfall structures mean they get 15-20% until investor achieves preferred return. Then they get catch-up. Reading and modeling the waterfall is CRITICAL.

Success Factors:

  • Detailed cash flow modeling (not just proforma profit)
  • Conservative market assumptions (longer absorption, lower prices than "base case")
  • Adequate capital or committed credit facility (2-3 years of carrying costs)
  • Partner alignment (investor must have patient capital, not "flip and run" mentality)
  • Phased development (don't build all 200 lots upfront - build 50, test market, then expand)

flashcards.question: What is the fundamental accounting difference between construction contracting and real estate development?
flashcards.answer: Contracting: Contract accounting (ASC 606) - recognize revenue OVER TIME as work is performed; balance sheet shows contract assets/liabilities. Development: Inventory accounting (ASC 360) - capitalize all costs to INVENTORY, recognize revenue AT SALE when control transfers; no revenue during development. Critical: Development does NOT use % completion for revenue - only when sold!

flashcards.question: What costs are capitalizable to real estate inventory during development?
flashcards.answer: Capitalize: (1) Acquisition costs (purchase price, closing, due diligence), (2) Pre-development (engineering, entitlements, permits, impact fees), (3) Development (clearing, grading, streets, utilities, landscaping), (4) Interest during development period. Do NOT capitalize: G&A overhead (unless traceable), marketing after sales begin, selling commissions, interest after substantially complete.

flashcards.question: How does interest capitalization work for real estate development?
flashcards.answer: ASC 835-20: Capitalize interest on construction loans DURING development period when (1) expenditures made, (2) development activities in progress, (3) interest incurred. Capitalization STOPS when substantially complete (ready for sale/use). Example: $327K during 8-month development = capitalize to inventory; $67K/month after completion = expense. Increases inventory cost per lot.

flashcards.question: What is the relative value method for lot cost allocation?
flashcards.answer: Allocate total development cost based on relative estimated SALES VALUES of lots. Formula: Lot Cost = (Lot Sales Value ÷ Total Sales Value) × Total Cost. Results in EQUAL gross profit % across all lot types. Example: Premium lots $500K (38.5% of total value) receive 38.5% of cost; Standard lots $225K (34.6%) receive 34.6% of cost → both achieve 23% margin.

flashcards.question: How are model homes accounted for?
flashcards.answer: If used primarily for MARKETING (not immediate sale): Capitalize as Property, Plant & Equipment; depreciate over useful life (3-5 years). When converting to inventory for sale: transfer at lower of NBV or NRV. If built with intent to SELL as inventory: capitalize as inventory from inception. Example: $450K model, 3-year life = $150K/year depreciation. Convert after 2 years: NBV $150K, sell for $380K = $230K gross profit.

flashcards.question: How are HOA common area costs and operating subsidies accounted for?
flashcards.answer: Common area costs (clubhouse, pool, parks): Capitalize to inventory, allocate to lots (e.g., $1.5M ÷ 200 lots = $7,500/lot). Flows through COGS when lots sold. HOA operating subsidies (after sales begin): Expense as period cost (HOA Subsidy Expense), not capitalizable. Developer subsidizes during sell-out when assessments < operating costs. At turnover (75-90% sold), transfer assets to homeowner-controlled HOA.

flashcards.question: When is revenue recognized for real estate lot sales under ASC 606?
flashcards.answer: Revenue recognized when CONTROL TRANSFERS, typically at closing. Requires: (1) Closing occurred (title transferred), (2) Adequate initial investment (10-25% down), (3) Receivable not subordinated, (4) Possession transferred, (5) No continuing involvement. If inadequate down payment, non-recourse financing, or buyback provisions = control NOT transferred → treat as deposit, defer revenue until contingencies resolve.

flashcards.question: What is a waterfall distribution structure in developer-investor JVs?
flashcards.answer: Typical 4-tier waterfall: (1) Return of capital - 100% to partners proportionately, (2) Preferred return - investor receives fixed % annual return (e.g., 12%) on unreturned capital, (3) Catch-up - developer receives 100% until achieving same % return as investor, (4) Promoted interest - remaining split (e.g., 70% investor / 30% developer). Developer receives disproportionate profit share (30% of profits despite 25% ownership) after investor achieves preferred return.

flashcards.question: What are the three lot cost allocation methods?
flashcards.answer: (1) Relative Value Method - based on sales values; results in equal GP% (most common). (2) Specific Identification - trace specific costs to lots/phases; used for distinct cost patterns. (3) Area Method - based on lot size (SF or acres); simple but ignores value differences. Choice affects gross profit by lot type and tax timing. Relative value best reflects economics (premium lots bear higher costs).

flashcards.question: Why do construction contractors fail in real estate development?
flashcards.answer: Top failures: (1) Cash flow ignorance - no progress billings, all cash upfront, 2-3 years before sales revenue. (2) Applying % completion to inventory - WRONG, creates phantom profit and tax. (3) Market timing - all-in with no exit if market turns. (4) Undercapitalized - can't fund share of cost overruns. (5) Waterfall misunderstanding - expect 40% profit, receive 20% until investor achieves preferred return. Success requires: detailed cash modeling, conservative assumptions, adequate capital, phased approach.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between construction contracting and real estate development accounting?
options: Both use percentage of completion (ASC 606)
Contracting uses contract accounting (revenue over time); Development uses inventory accounting (revenue at sale)
Development recognizes revenue faster than contracting
Contracting capitalizes costs; Development expenses costs
quiz.explanation: Construction contractors use ASC 606 contract accounting (recognize revenue over time as work is performed). Real estate developers use ASC 360 inventory accounting (capitalize all costs to inventory, recognize revenue at point of sale when control transfers). This is a critical distinction - development projects do NOT recognize revenue using % completion as they're built; revenue is recognized only when lots/homes are SOLD.

quiz.question: Which of the following costs should NOT be capitalized to real estate inventory during land development?
options: Engineering and platting fees
Interest on construction loans during development
Marketing and advertising costs after sales begin
Impact fees and development assessments
quiz.explanation: ASC 970-360-25: Capitalize costs directly related to acquisition and development (purchase price, pre-development, infrastructure, interest during development). Marketing and advertising AFTER sales begin are period costs (expensed as incurred), not capitalizable. Selling commissions and closing costs are also expensed. Once development is substantially complete and sales begin, capitalization stops.

quiz.question: A developer spends $10M developing 150 lots. Interest on the construction loan during the 8-month development period is $327K. After development is substantially complete (Month 9), monthly interest is $67K. How should the interest be treated?
options: All $327K + $67K capitalized to inventory
$327K capitalized; $67K expensed (development complete)
All interest expensed (interest is never capitalizable)
$327K expensed; $67K capitalized
quiz.explanation: ASC 835-20: Capitalize interest during the development period when (1) expenditures made, (2) development activities in progress, and (3) interest incurred. Capitalization STOPS when development is substantially complete. The $327K during Months 1-8 is capitalized to inventory ($10,327K total cost ÷ 150 lots = $68,847 per lot). The $67K in Month 9+ is expensed as Interest Expense.

quiz.question: Using the relative value method, allocate $5M total cost to: 10 premium lots ($250K each = $2.5M total value), 20 standard lots ($180K each = $3.6M total value). What is the cost per premium lot?
options: $250,000 (sales price)
$204,918 (relative value allocation)
quiz.explanation: Relative value method allocates cost based on relative sales values. Total estimated sales: $2.5M + $3.6M = $6.1M. Premium allocation: ($2.5M / $6.1M) × $5M = 40.98% × $5M = $2,049,180 total. Per lot: $2,049,180 ÷ 10 = $204,918. This results in equal gross profit percentage across all lot types (Standard: $180K - $147,541 = 18.1% margin; Premium: $250K - $204,918 = 18.1% margin).

quiz.question: A model home is built for $450K (including $75K lot) to serve as a sales model for 3 years. How should it initially be accounted for?
options: Real estate inventory (will be sold)
Property, Plant & Equipment (depreciate over 3 years)
Marketing expense (expensed immediately)
Intangible asset (amortize over 3 years)
quiz.explanation: ASC 360-10-35: Model homes used primarily for marketing are capitalized as Property, Plant & Equipment and depreciated over useful life (typically 3-5 years). Entry: DR: Model Home - PP&E $450K; CR: Cash $450K. Annual depreciation: $150K ($450K ÷ 3 years). When converted to inventory for sale, transfer at lower of net book value or net realizable value. If built with intent to sell as inventory (not primarily marketing), capitalize as inventory from inception.

quiz.question: A model home with original cost $450K has accumulated depreciation of $300K (NBV $150K). It's converted to inventory and sold for $380K. What is the gross profit?
options: $380,000 (100% - NBV is $0 after full depreciation)
($70,000) loss ($450K cost - $380K sale)
quiz.explanation: Transfer model from PP&E to inventory at lower of NBV ($150K) or NRV ($380K) = $150K. Entry: DR: Inventory $150K, DR: Accum Depr $300K; CR: Model Home $450K. Upon sale: DR: Cash $380K; CR: Revenue $380K; DR: COGS $150K; CR: Inventory $150K. Gross profit: $380K - $150K = $230K (60.5% margin). The prior $300K depreciation was expensed in previous years; only remaining NBV becomes inventory cost.

quiz.question: A developer creates an HOA and builds $1.5M in common area amenities (clubhouse, pool, parks) for a 200-home community. How should the $1.5M be accounted for initially?
options: Expense immediately as marketing costs
Capitalize to PP&E and depreciate
Capitalize to real estate inventory and allocate to lots ($7,500 per lot)
Record as loan to HOA
quiz.explanation: Common area costs are development costs that benefit all lots, so capitalize to real estate inventory and allocate to individual lots. Entry: DR: Real Estate Inventory $1.5M; CR: Cash $1.5M. Allocation: $1.5M ÷ 200 lots = $7,500 per lot. Each lot's total cost includes its share of common areas. When lots are sold, the $7,500 flows through COGS. At HOA turnover (typically 75-90% sold), transfer remaining common area assets to homeowner-controlled HOA.

quiz.question: During HOA sell-out phase, homeowners pay $60K in assessments but HOA operating costs are $120K. The developer subsidizes the $60K deficit. How should the developer account for the subsidy?
options: Capitalize to real estate inventory (development cost)
Expense as period cost (HOA Subsidy Expense)
Loan to HOA (receivable)
No entry - developer has no obligation
quiz.explanation: HOA subsidies incurred AFTER lots are ready for sale are period costs (expensed as incurred), not capitalizable to inventory. Entry: DR: HOA Subsidy Expense $60K; CR: Cash $60K. This is expensed on the income statement, reducing current period profit. Capitalization ended when development was substantially complete. Subsidies during sell-out are common because fewer homeowners are paying assessments while full amenity costs continue.

quiz.question: Under ASC 606, when should revenue be recognized for a lot sale to a homebuilder?
options: When the sales contract is signed
When the lot is finished and ready for construction
At closing, when control transfers (adequate down payment, no contingencies)
When the homebuilder completes construction on the lot
quiz.explanation: ASC 606-10-55-8: Revenue from real estate sales is recognized when control transfers, typically at closing. Control transfer indicators: (1) closing occurred (title transferred), (2) adequate initial investment (10-25% of sales price), (3) receivable not subject to subordination, (4) possession transferred, (5) no continuing involvement. If 'sale' has inadequate down payment, non-recourse financing, or buyback provisions, control hasn't transferred - treat as deposit, defer revenue.

quiz.question: What is a 'promoted interest' in a developer-investor joint venture?
options: The developer's initial equity contribution
An incentive bonus paid for early project completion
A disproportionate profit share the developer receives after investor achieves preferred return
Marketing fees paid to the developer
quiz.explanation: Promoted interest (or 'carry') is the developer's disproportionate share of profits in the final tier of a waterfall structure. Example: Developer has 25% ownership but receives 30-50% of profits in the final tier after investor receives: (1) return of capital, (2) preferred return (e.g., 12% annually), and (3) developer catch-up to match investor's return. The promoted interest compensates the developer for expertise and sweat equity with less capital at risk.

quiz.question: In a waterfall distribution, investor contributed $15M, developer contributed $5M. After return of capital ($20M) and preferred return ($7.2M to investor), what is the 'catch-up' tier?
options: Split remaining profit based on ownership % (75%/25%)
Developer receives 100% until achieving same % return as investor
Investor continues receiving 100% until capital doubled
No further distribution - all cash distributed
quiz.explanation: The catch-up tier gives the developer 100% of the next profits until their return percentage matches the investor's. Example: Investor received 48% return ($7.2M pref return on $15M). Developer needs 48% × $5M = $2.4M to match. Developer receives 100% of the next $2.4M. After catch-up, both have achieved same % return, and remaining profits split per promoted interest (e.g., 70% investor / 30% developer).

quiz.question: Which lot cost allocation method results in equal gross profit percentages across all lot types?
options: Area method (based on lot size)
Specific identification method
Relative value method (based on sales prices)
FIFO method
quiz.explanation: The relative value method allocates costs in proportion to estimated sales values, resulting in equal gross profit percentages for all lot types. Example: Total cost $5M, total sales $6.5M = 23.1% margin. Each lot type receives 23.1% margin (Premium: $500K - $384,615 = 23.1%; Standard: $350K - $269,231 = 23.1%). Area method results in unequal margins because it doesn't reflect value differences. Specific identification can result in varying margins.

quiz.question: A developer sells a lot for $150K with $5K down (3.3%) and $145K non-recourse seller note. Buyer can rescind within 12 months. Should revenue be recognized?
options: Yes - contract is signed, recognize full $150K
Yes - recognize $5K (cash collected)
No - control hasn't transferred; treat as deposit
Yes - recognize $150K less reserve for cancellation
quiz.explanation: Control has NOT transferred because: (1) initial investment inadequate (3.3% vs. required 10-25%), (2) non-recourse note means seller retains risk, (3) rescission provision = contingent sale. Entry: DR: Cash $5K; CR: Deposit Liability $5K. Lot remains in inventory. Do NOT recognize revenue. When buyer pays more and contingencies resolve (e.g., 12 months later after home is built), THEN recognize revenue. Premature revenue recognition creates phantom profit and tax liability without cash.

quiz.question: Interest capitalization on a development project STOPS when:
options: The construction loan is paid off
Development is substantially complete and ready for intended use
The developer decides to stop capitalizing
All lots are sold
quiz.explanation: ASC 835-20: Interest capitalization stops when the asset is substantially complete and ready for its intended use (i.e., lots are ready for sale or home construction). After this point, interest is expensed as Interest Expense. The loan may still be outstanding (and accruing interest), but it's no longer capitalizable. Timing matters: $67K/month interest capitalized during development increases inventory cost; expensed after completion reduces current period income.

quiz.question: Why do many construction contractors fail when they enter real estate development?
options: Lack of construction expertise
Applying contract accounting (% completion) to inventory, creating phantom profit
Overestimating construction costs
Building better quality than required
quiz.explanation: The #1 accounting mistake: Contractors mistakenly apply percentage of completion accounting to development projects, recognizing 'revenue' as lots are developed (e.g., 50% complete = 50% of revenue). This is WRONG. Development uses inventory accounting - NO revenue until lots are SOLD. Mistakes create: (1) phantom profit, (2) accelerated tax liability with no cash, (3) debt covenant violations, (4) cash crunches. Other failures: undercapitalization, market timing disasters, misunderstanding waterfall structures.
